research.abstract: ABSTRACT Listeria monocytogenes is a Gram-positive bacterial foodborne pathogen responsible for the severe illness listeriosis. Of the 14 L. monocytogenes serotypes, serotype 4b is a major contributor to human listeriosis and encompasses all four leading hypervirulent clonal complexes (CCs), including the ancient, ubiquitous CC2. CC2 is globally dominated by sublineage (SL) 2, responsible for most human CC2-associated cases. Here we describe two other CC2 SLs, SLs 782 and 1039. These SLs are newly recognized, having been reported only since 2002, and to date are encountered exclusively in North America. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that they are strikingly divergent from each other as well as from SL2. SL782 and SL1039 have been implicated in human listeriosis and have also been repeatedly isolated from surface water and wildlife in North America, with several of these environmental strains exhibiting high genomic similarity (≤7 core genome allelic mismatches) to strains from human listeriosis. They share an unusual resistance profile towards a panel of Listeria wide-host-range-phages and exhibit several distinct lineage-specific traits. Specifically, SL782 universally lacks a gene otherwise unique to and conserved in serotype 4b and harbors the Listeria pathogenicity island LIPI-4, while SL1039 harbors LIPI-3 and is almost always resistant to tetracycline, harboring the novel Tn 916 -like transposon Tn 916 . 1039 . These and other traits may have driven clonal emergence of SL782 and SL1039, potentially via adaptations in natural ecosystems. IMPORTANCE Listeria monocytogenes causes the severe foodborne illness listeriosis and the hypervirulent clonal complex (CC) 2 is a major contributor to human disease. Most CC2 strains belong to the long-recognized, ubiquitous sublineage (SL) 2. Surprisingly, the two other leading SLs within CC2, SL782 and 1039, have been isolated exclusively from North America, and only subsequently to 2002. They differ remarkably from each other and other CC2 strains and exhibit unusual genomic and phenotypic traits. They have been repeatedly isolated from watersheds and wildlife, with such environmental isolates exhibiting high genomic similarity to those from human listeriosis. The findings are important in identifying novel, unexpected features in the composition and evolution of a major, hypervirulent L. monocytogenes CC. They will also serve as platforms for further studies to further elucidate the reservoirs, emergence, persistence, and dissemination of novel Listeria sublineages and their roles in the continuum between natural ecosystems and human disease.

research.abstract: Introduction Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical threat to global health security and disproportionately affects children in sub-Saharan Africa. In Nigeria, the burden of multidrug-resistant pathogens in paediatric populations is increasing; however, data from the South-South region, particularly Edo State, remain scarce. This study aims to determine the prevalence, patterns and transmission dynamics of AMR among paediatric patients in Edo State, Nigeria, using a One Health approach that integrates human, animal and environmental health interfaces. Methods and analysis This mixed-methods study will enrol 455 hospitalised children (<18 years) at the University of Benin Teaching Hospital (UBTH). Clinical (urine, blood, rectal and nasopharyngeal swabs), environmental and animal samples will be collected to isolate and characterise locally recoverable bacterial pathogens prioritised with reference to the WHO 2024 priority pathogen list. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing will be performed using the Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion method in accordance with Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute guidelines. Selected clinically or epidemiologically important resistant isolates will be stored at -80°C for possible future molecular characterisation, resources permitting. Key informant interviews with caregivers, healthcare providers and policymakers will explore the systemic enablers and barriers to paediatric AMR stewardship. Quantitative data will be analysed using descriptive statistics and logistic regression, while qualitative data will undergo thematic analysis guided by Braun and Clarke's framework. Ethics and dissemination Ethical approval has been obtained from the UBTH Health Research Ethics Committee (Ref: ADM/E 22/A/VOL.VII/14831247). Written informed consent will be obtained from all participants. Findings will inform antibiotic stewardship, strengthen surveillance and guide AMR policy at institutional, state and national levels. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, policy briefs, institutional reports and engagement with national and international health agencies.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is associated with various adverse outcomes, but links with subsequent violent victimisation are uncertain. Methods We linked data from Swedish sociodemographic and medical registers to create a matched cohort of people with diagnosed PTSD and a comparison sample matched on birth year, sex, and county of residence in the year preceding diagnosis (or matching in the case of undiagnosed individuals). We calculated the cumulative incidence of violent victimisation (defined using ICD codes registered at hospitalisation) and conducted stratified Cox regression analyses, adjusted for parental factors, psychiatric comorbidities, and history of violent victimisation. Findings The cohort contained 29,688 individuals diagnosed with PTSD, who were matched with 296,880 individuals without PTSD (78.6% female), and followed for up to 34 years. Individuals with PTSD had higher cumulative incidences of violent victimisation after their index diagnosis (18.7% compared to 2.7% at 25 years follow-up). Individuals with both a diagnosis of PTSD and history of violent victimisation had the highest cumulative incidence (28.7%). After adjustment for parental characteristics, prior psychiatric comorbidity and prior violent victimisation, PTSD was associated with an adjusted hazard ratio of 4.0 (95% CI 3.7–4.4). Interpretation Preventing subsequent violent victimisation among individuals diagnosed with PTSD should be considered by clinical services and incorporated into violence prevention strategies. research.abstract: INTRODUCTION: TB (tuberculosis) due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis continues to be a significant worldwide health issue. Timely and reliable diagnostic tests will improve treatment outcomes and reduce the spread of disease. Traditional TB diagnostics currently available, such as smear microscopy and culture, have significant limitations with regard to sensitivity and turnaround times, especially for smear-negative cases and for tuberculosis in extrapulmonary locations. OBJECTIVES: The purpose of this review is to analyze the evolution of TB diagnostics from traditional microbiology to new molecular diagnostic methods (including CRISPR, biosensor technology, and microfluidic methods), including an assessment of their diagnostic testing performance, feasibility, and potential for the future. METHODS: The systematic narrative review aimed to systematically assess literature published from 2020 to 2025 retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. The review was carried out according to the PRISMA guidelines and included 89 studies after screening and assessing for eligibility. The data were analysed qualitatively (i.e., through thematic analysis) by comparing data from conventional, molecular, and next-generation diagnostic methods. RESULTS: Molecular tests (e.g., GeneXpert, Line Probe Assays, PCR, and Whole Genome Sequencing) provide greater sensitivity and specificity than traditional methods and allow for faster diagnosis. Additionally, newer CRISPR-based tests, biosensors, and microfluidic devices hold promise for rapid, portable, point-of-care diagnosis of tuberculosis. DISCUSSION: The findings indicate that molecular diagnostics improve rapid detection and drug-resistance profiling, while CRISPR and biosensor platforms offer potential for rapid point-of-care testing. However, affordability, infrastructure, clinical validation, and scalability remain important barriers. CONCLUSION: The use of molecular diagnostic testing, CRISPR technology, biosensors, artificial intelligence, and portable platforms will dramatically enhance existing TB surveillance systems and strategies for controlling the disease globally.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis , remains a major global health challenge, further exacerbated by the rapid emergence of drug-resistant strains. Despite continuous efforts, the discovery of novel anti-TB agents has lagged behind the evolution of resistance, largely due to the limitations of conventional experimental pipelines and the growing biological complexity of the pathogen. In recent years, computational drug discovery approaches—including virtual screening, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven modeling, and hybrid computational frameworks—have substantially expanded the chemical space accessible for early-stage anti-TB research. However, their translational success remains limited. This discrepancy reflects a fundamental mismatch between target-centric computational paradigms and the multi-scale biological constraints of Mtb , including permeability barriers, efflux mechanisms, metabolic state heterogeneity, lesion-level pharmacokinetics, and regimen-dependent therapeutic effects. This review critically evaluates current computational strategies for anti-TB drug screening, with particular emphasis on their performance under TB-specific biological and resistance constraints. We further explore computational approaches designed to address drug-resistant Mtb , including resistance-aware compound design, host-directed therapy, and combination regimen modeling. Finally, we explore key limitations in current computational pipelines, including challenges in data quality, biological integration, and regimen-level modeling, and propose a shift toward biologically grounded, regimen-aware, and systems-level frameworks. Bridging the gap between in silico prediction and clinical efficacy will require integrating multi-scale biological realism into computational pipelines, enabling more reliable translation of computational advances into effective anti-TB therapeutics.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Species in the Rosaceae tribe Spiraeeae occupy diverse habitats and vary strikingly in growth form and leaf morphology. Still, no reference transcriptomes have been published for the tribe, and its transcriptome‐level variation is uncharacterized. We generated long‐read (PacBio Iso‐Seq) reference transcriptomes of five species spanning three genera: Petrophytum caespitosum (Nutt.) Rydb., Spiraea lucida Douglas ex Greene, Spiraea splendens Baumann ex K. Koch, Aruncus dioicus (Walter) Fernald var. dioicus , and Aruncus aethusifolius (H.Lév.) Nakai. We then quantified expression across 20 individuals using 3′‐tag RNA sequencing (TagSeq) to characterize expression patterns, ortholog sequence divergence, and gene repertoire. Multivariate analyses (principal component analysis [PCA] and hierarchical clustering) resolved replicates into three groups corresponding to the sampled genera. Because the material combined field‐collected and potted plants, we treat expression comparisons as descriptive and do not attribute them to genetic control of interspecific differences. Pairwise analyses revealed extensive transcriptional divergence between genera, including thousands of differentially expressed transcripts in comparisons such as A. aethusifolius vs. P. caespitosum . Functional enrichment highlighted variation in transport and catabolism, plastid organization, and biotic‐stress responses, implicating both metabolic and organelle‐associated processes. Transcription factor families, particularly bHLH and bZIP, varied most among differentially expressed transcripts. Weighted gene coexpression network analysis (WGCNA) recovered modules correlated with species identity; because between‐species variation dominates this dataset, we treat these as descriptive summaries of coexpression structure and do not regard them as independent evidence of species‐specific regulatory programs. Because reads were quantified against a reference assembled from species‐specific contigs, mapping rates were higher within species (70.5%–85.1%) than across species (25.1%–77.0%), and between‐species expression comparisons are interpreted with this asymmetry in mind. Sequence‐level analysis of orthologous transcript pairs indicated that protein‐coding genes are predominantly under purifying selection. A small fraction (2.7%–5.0% of retained pairs) showed Ka/Ks > 1, but these were concentrated at low synonymous divergence, where ratio estimates are unstable; we therefore treat them as screening‐level candidates for rapid divergence, enriched for stress‐response, membrane‐trafficking, and ion‐transport annotations, and we make no claim of positive selection. These results provide a comparative transcriptomic framework for Spiraeeae and identify candidate transcripts and protein‐coding differences for future studies of ecological and morphological variation in Rosaceae.

research.abstract: Computing phylogenetic likelihoods becomes challenging when the continuous-time Markov chain has a large state space. At each branch, pruning algorithms require terms of the form $e^{Q t}\cdot B$, where $Q$ is an $S \times S$ rate matrix (e.g., for $S$ states), $t$ is a branch length, and the columns of matrix $B$ (e.g., $B \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{S \times L}$) are partial-likelihood vectors for $L$ site patterns. Many implementations calculate the dense transition matrix $P(t)=e^{Q t}$ via eigendecomposition and multiply it by $B$. This strategy is efficient for small state spaces, but it can be inefficient for large sparse rate matrices because forming $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices destroys sparsity and its cost may not be well amortized when $L$ is small. We implement an alternative likelihood kernel based on the Al-Mohy and Higham (2011) algorithm for computing the action of the matrix exponential directly, avoiding explicit construction of $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices. The resulting method takes full advantage of the sparsity of $Q$. We implement this method as a CPU-based extension to the BEAGLE library and evaluate it on two large-state molecular models: a Markov-modulated codon model of heterotachy with $M$ selective regimes and $61\cdot M$ possible states, and a codon-pair model of interlocus gene conversion between two paralogs with $61^2=3\,721$ possible states. Our results characterize when action-based likelihood computation improves performance over calculating $e^{Q t}$ directly. We show that this method enables fast, scalable inference for complex models, removing a key computational barrier to the study of evolution with large state space models.

research.abstract: Extrapulmonary tuberculosis (EPTB) contributes significantly to the global tuberculosis burden, yet treatment response and drug resistance remain poorly characterized. India, a high- tuberculosis burden country, faces growing challenges of delayed diagnosis, treatment and drug-resistant tuberculosis, particularly in extrapulmonary forms. This study evaluated early clinical response to therapy and identified factors associated with rifampicin resistance among patients with EPTB. A prospective observational study was conducted at a tertiary care centre in central India between 2018 and 2024. A total of 532 patients with microbiologically confirmed EPTB, based on the Xpert MTB/RIF assay, were included. The study collected baseline demographic, clinical, and laboratory data. Clinical response at 8 weeks was assessed using standardized criteria. Multivariable logistic regression analysis identified factors associated with slow clinical response and rifampicin resistance. A total of 5,764 presumptive EPTB samples were tested using the Xpert MTB/RIF assay. Among these, 532 patients had confirmed EPTB. Rifampicin resistance was detected in 36 patients (6.7%), while 496 patients had rifampicin-sensitive disease and were included in the response analysis. Among these patients, 113 (22.8%) demonstrated slow clinical response. Slow response showed independent association with HIV co-infection, diabetes mellitus, malnutrition, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, prolonged symptom duration, and non-lymph node disease, particularly abdominal and genitourinary tuberculosis. Socioeconomic factors, such as rural residence and lower educational status, also showed independent association. Elevated inflammatory markers, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, showed independent association with slow clinical response. Rifampicin resistance showed independent association with previous tuberculosis, HIV infection, male sex, and disseminated disease. A significant overlap existed between delayed clinical response and drug resistance, as rifampicin resistance occurred more frequently among slow responders than among responders (12.3% vs. 4.1%, p = 0.002). Nearly one-quarter of patients with EPTB demonstrated delayed clinical response at 8 weeks. Both host-related and disease-related factors showed association with treatment response, while rifampicin resistance showed strong association with prior tuberculosis and immunosuppression. The overlap between slow clinical response and drug resistance highlighted the importance of early molecular diagnostics and targeted clinical monitoring in high-risk patients.

research.abstract: Human Y chromosome satellites vary widely but remain difficult to measure in large cohorts. We developed Yruler, which uses pangenome assemblies to measure satellite lengths, composition and Y dosage from sequencing reads without alignment. Across cohorts, we find lineage-associated differences in centromere and non-centromeric array length, and show that heterochromatin components vary unequally within lineages. Yruler enables population-scale studies of how Y satellite variation relates to health and disease.

research.abstract: Coupled Metropolis-Hastings MCMC sampling (runie-mcmc-skyline: G = 10,000 generations, 20% burn-in = 2,000 discarded, 8,000 posterior states) across 64 ancient/modern hominin mitogenomes and 16 nuclear loci (L = 87,227 *MAFFT / 86,612 Native Rust gotoh-msa aligned bp) resolving the 5-stage Neanderthal Ne(t) collapse (13,893 to 602.7 at 39.2 ka BP) and 37.3x speedup over *MAFFT + *IQ-TREE + *BEAST v1.10.4 Reconstructing the demographic trajectory and extinction timing of archaic hominins from ancient DNA requires separating genuine coalescent bottlenecks from post-mortem cytosine deamination and nuclear pseudogene artifacts while jointly estimating tree topology, divergence dates, and effective population size over time. Here we introduce and validate a configurable long-form Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler inside the Rust Native Inference Engine (runie-mcmc-skyline; default 10,000 generations with a 20% burn-in gate) and benchmark it against *BEAST, *IQ-TREE with *LSD2, and *PAML codeml across an 87,227-bp hominin alignment spanning Neanderthals, Denisovans, Sima de los Huesos, and modern humans. Sampling the stationary posterior distribution reconstructs a five-stage Neanderthal demographic collapse from a Middle Pleistocene effective population size of 13,893 down to 603 breeding individuals at the 39.2 ka extinction horizon, driven by recurring glacial bottlenecks, consanguineous inbreeding, and a three-fold relaxation of mitochondrial purifying selection. Finally, stage-level timing comparisons demonstrate that Native Rust completes alignment and 10,000-generation MCMC sampling 37.3-fold faster than the external *MAFFT, *IQ-TREE, and *BEAST tool chain while preventing the 22.3-fold false terminal population inflation caused by uncleaned ancient-DNA deamination. research.abstract: Phylogenetic trees are hybrid objects: branch lengths vary continuously, while topologies change discretely through edge contractions and expansions. Billera-Holmes-Vogtmann (BHV) tree space provides a canonical geometry for this structure, representing each resolved topology as a Euclidean orthant and topological changes as motion across shared lower-dimensional boundaries. We introduce PhylaFlow, a hybrid flow-matching model that learns posterior-basin transport in BHV tree space. PhylaFlow is trained on BHV geodesic paths from random starting trees to short-run posterior samples, coupling continuous branch-length motion within orthants with learned boundary events and discrete topology transitions. We evaluate the learned geometry operationally: if the flow reaches posterior-relevant regions, finite-budget Bayesian refinement initialized from, or guided by, its terminal trees should recover posterior-supported topologies more efficiently. Across DS1-DS8 phylogenetic posterior benchmarks, PhylaFlow substantially reduces initial Tree-KL relative to classical initializers. After finite-budget MrBayes refinement, direct PhylaFlow improves early and intermediate topology-recovery trajectories on most datasets, while split-guided PhylaFlow-MCMC obtains the strongest hard-case results. The best PhylaFlow variant outperforms short-warmup on seven of eight datasets and PhyloGFN on five of eight under the same refinement budget. In a joint sequence-conditioned experiment, sequence embeddings steer posterior split recovery, although exact posterior topology recovery remains preliminary. These results show that hybrid flow matching can learn actionable transport in BHV tree space and provide a geometry-aware proposal mechanism for Bayesian phylogenetic inference.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Chromosome replication initiation in bacterial genomes typically occurs at a single origin, called oriC, through the binding of the DnaA initiator protein to specific chromosomal repeats known as DnaA-boxes. Here, relying on comparative genomics, we show that the family Fusobacteriaceae, which belongs to the order Fusobacteriales alongside the family Leptotrichiaceae, deviates from this paradigm. Our analysis revealed a stark contrast between the two lineages: while dnaA flanks oriC in Leptotrichiaceae, it is notably missing from Fusobacteriaceae genomes. Adjacent to oriC in Fusobacteriaceae, we identified a gene encoding replication initiator protein A (RPA). We characterized RPA as a Rep-type initiator involved in plasmid replication that likely originated from an iteron-containing plasmid, iterons being the plasmid analogues of DnaA-boxes. Phylogenetic reconstruction indicates that the gene encoding RPA was acquired together with its associated iterons and subsequently domesticated by the Fusobacteriaceae ancestor, successfully displacing the ancestral chromosomal dnaA gene at the origin of replication. This shift to a plasmid-derived replication system may represent an adaptive trait of the Fusobacteriaceae, potentially offering new insights into the biology of Fusobacterium nucleatum , a member of this family known to be a major driver of colorectal cancer progression within the tumor microenvironment.

research.abstract: Abstract This perspective provides an overview of what we know from real-world data on reversal of drug resistance evolution. An important question for those who study drug resistance is whether it is possible to reverse the evolution of resistance, for example by halting the use of specific drugs for a patient or even a community or country. Evidence for successful reversal of resistance levels is spread out in many different subfields of infectious disease. I use examples from P. falciparum malaria, several bacterial species including E. coli, M. tuberculosis, and S. aureus, and the viral pathogen HIV, to show that it is possible to reverse the evolution of resistance.

items.title: The dynamics of gene copy-number mutations: transient changes with long-lasting consequences.
items.summary: Gene copy-number mutations are frequent and prevalent yet often overlooked. While initially considered to be the neutrally evolving raw material needed for the emergence of new genes through the process of gene duplication and divergence, recent technical advances and renewed interest start to unravel a fundamentally different picture for duplications in bacteria: rather than being neutral…

research.abstract: Abstract Gene copy-number mutations are frequent and prevalent yet often overlooked. While initially considered to be the neutrally evolving raw material needed for the emergence of new genes through the process of gene duplication and divergence, recent technical advances and renewed interest start to unravel a fundamentally different picture for duplications in bacteria: rather than being neutral, duplications have strong direct and indirect fitness effects, and rather than giving rise to evolutionary novelty through protein family expansions, duplications allow to transiently simply make more of the same. Tandem duplications arise at frequencies orders of magnitude higher than single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), and they collapse at an even higher rate still. Understanding the biological idiosyncrasies of copy-number mutations is pivotal to understanding their fundamental role in bacterial evolution. Having multiple copies of a gene influences its evolutionary dynamics in surprising ways, slowing down divergence, acting along with purifying selection as a force of conservation, and facilitating “bet-hedging” in fluctuating environments or under diversifying selection. Paying careful attention to structural variation in genomic sequence analyses will yield a more comprehensive understanding of bacterial evolution, especially when it comes to the emergence of novel bacterial lineages, such as human pathogens.

research.abstract: Characium and Characium -like algae represent a taxonomically challenging group within Chlorophyceae. Due to their high phenotypic plasticity and convergent morphology, their true evolutionary relationships have long remained unresolved, and the lack of genomic resources has further hindered taxonomic revision. We sequenced and assembled seven complete chloroplast genomes from Characium and morphologically similar taxa and documented their detailed cell morphology. Comparative genomic analyses revealed that while most genomes retained the typical quadripartite structure, they exhibited significant structural variation, including gene rearrangements and diverse IR expansions/contractions. Furthermore, phylogenetic analyses based on 64 protein-coding genes successfully resolved the long-standing taxonomic ambiguity of Characium and Characium -like algae, placing the strains into three distinct, well-supported clades within Sphaeropleales and Volvocales. The synteny patterns and DCJ distances were consistent with the phylogeny: closely related species showed largely conserved gene order and low DCJ distances, whereas more distant lineages exhibited extensive rearrangements and higher distances. Branch-site tests identified a small set of positively selected genes, mainly related to photosynthesis, proteolysis, and plastid gene expression, suggesting that adaptive processes may have contributed to chloroplast genome diversity in these algae. This study establishes the first clear phylogenomic framework for these lineages, revealing distinct evolutionary patterns of gene loss and structural rearrangement that align with the newly resolved clades. It also provides an important basis for advancing studies on chloroplast genome evolution within Chlorophyceae.

research.abstract: Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) presents a significant therapeutic challenge due to increasing multidrug resistance (MDR). While acquired resistance mechanisms are well-documented, the genetic variability of intrinsic efflux pumps like EmrD remains less characterized. This study investigated the genomic diversity and structural conservation of the EmrD transporter in ten clinical MDR isolates from the Kurdistan Region, Iraq. Isolates were screened for the emrD and β-lactamase genes, followed by emrD sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and in silico protein modeling. Results confirmed the universal presence of emrD alongside multiple resistance genes. Phylogenetic analysis identified notable local genetic diversity, including a highly divergent lineage (DUH 11). Protein modeling mapped non-synonymous substitutions to transmembrane helices 6 and 12, regions critical for the "rocker-switch" conformational changes required for substrate translocation. These findings suggest that while EmrD is a stable component of the MDR machinery, localized genomic divergence may potentially influence efflux efficiency among clinical lineages, warranting future functional validation.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis remains challenging, particularly for extrapulmonary TB (EPTB), where invasive sampling, low bacillary burden, and limited sensitivity of nucleic acid-based tests in peripheral specimens hinder timely detection. Here, we report an immunology-driven strategy for biomarker discovery and development of a peptide-based serological assay targeting Mycobacterium tuberculosis zinc metalloprotease-1 (Zmp1). Based on the principle that antigenic regions containing overlapping B-cell and CD4⁺T-cell epitopes can promote strong antibody responses through linked recognition and cognate T-cell help, we used an immunoinformatics pipeline to identify two nested immunodominant Zmp1 peptide regions, Mtb-Zp-NT and Mtb-Zp-CT, enriched for overlapping B- and T-cell epitopes.Their diagnostic potential was evaluated using ELISA-based serological assays. A blinded pilot study (N = 137) demonstrated clear discrimination between active TB and TB-recovered individuals. An expanded validation cohort (N = 875), identified from screening approximately 6,086 individuals, included pulmonary TB (PTB), EPTB, TB-recovered individuals, household contacts, non-specific infection/inflammation, and healthy controls. Receiver operating characteristic analyses, supported by DeLong and bootstrap comparisons, demonstrated superior diagnostic performance of the peptide assays compared with Mtb-FL-Zmp1. Mtb-Zp-CT showed the highest accuracy (AUC = 0.93), with > 93% specificity and ~ 76% sensitivity.These findings establish immunologically optimized Zmp1 peptides as promising serological biomarkers for TB, including EPTB. Although further optimization may be required to meet WHO target product profiles, their high specificity supports potential use as an adjunctive diagnostic, particularly for EPTB, and as components of future multi-antigen panels. More broadly, this study demonstrates how mechanistically informed epitope selection can facilitate translation of pathogen-specific immune signatures into minimally invasive diagnostic platforms.

research.abstract: Abstract Background The Streptococcus anginosus group (SAG) ( S. anginosus, S. intermedius, and S. constellatus ) causes serious, potentially life-threatening, invasive infections, often in otherwise healthy individuals. However, the group’s diversity is still poorly understood, and with it, the ability to identify prognostic markers of severe disease. Methods Long-read sequencing produced closed genomes for 29 isolates from 25 patients hospitalised primarily for invasive SAG infections, and 21 isolates from 20 non-hospitalised controls. Genomes were classified with GTDB-Tk and combined with 211 reference genomes. After dereplication, 207 SAG genomes (38 isolate, 169 reference) representing 206 strains were analysed using: GTDB classification, average nucleotide identity, multi-marker and core-genome SNP phylogenies, recombination-aware analyses, mobilome, CAZyme and gapseq metabolic profiling, and lineage-aware genome-wide association testing for invasive phenotype. Results Agreement between GTDB-Tk and MALDI-TOF taxonomic classifications was low (42.8%), including two S. massiliensis cases mis-identified by MALDI-TOF as SAG. S. anginosus resolved into four taxa ( S. anginosus , S. hominis , S. whileyi and S. vaginalis ). Phylogenies based on core genome single-nucleotide polymorphisms resolved these species into distinct clades, whereas 16S rRNA gene and multilocus sequence analysis phylogenies did not. The four ex- S. anginosus taxa showed a gradient of genomic cohesion, with S. vaginalis being near-clonal, in contrast to S. anginosus, which shared high levels of sequence ancestry with other neighbouring taxa. Carbohydrate utilisation was strongly lineage-associated, as was propensity for invasive disease. A ∼15Kbp glycosaminoglycan utilisation locus was found in the three taxa of highest disease severity propensity ( S. intermedius, S. constellatus, S. whileyi ) which predicts a direct host glycosaminoglycan feeding mechanism that may contribute to invasive disease. No single functional feature, gene or core-genome SNP was associated with invasiveness however after lineage-adjustment. Combined feature analysis suggests S. vaginalis has undergone a niche restriction and has evolved for a primary existence in the female urogenital tract. Conclusions Under-reported species may be mis-diagnosed as SAG invasive infections. SAG is more diverse than its current three-species definition, with the conventional S. anginosus species proposed to be classed into a complex of four distinct taxa. Invasive capacity appears to be an emergent system-level property rather than from individual features.

items.title: Multi-objective domain adaptation for pan-cancer transfer of pharmacogenomic drug response to patient tumours
items.summary: Large-scale pharmacogenomic screens provide rich drug-sensitivity measurements in cancer cell lines, but transferring these measurements to patient tumours remains limited by biological heterogeneity and cross-domain distribution shift. Existing machine learning approaches, including adversarial autoencoder and domain adaptation, address this gap by learning shared latent representations between…

research.abstract: Large-scale pharmacogenomic screens provide rich drug-sensitivity measurements in cancer cell lines, but transferring these measurements to patient tumours remains limited by biological heterogeneity and cross-domain distribution shift. Existing machine learning approaches, including adversarial autoencoder and domain adaptation, address this gap by learning shared latent representations between preclinical models and patient samples. However, alignment without explicit biological constraints can produce unreliable representations when cancer lineage structure and clinically relevant patient heterogeneity are not preserved. Here, we introduce MODAE+, a pan-cancer multi-objective deep learning domain adaptation framework that jointly balances domain alignment, deconfounding, drug-response prediction, survival prediction, and cancer-lineage classification across 9,696 TCGA tumours, 1,293 CCLE cancer cell lines, and CTRP sensitivity profiles for 544 compounds in 738 matched cell lines. This multi-objective design improved cross-domain alignment while preserving cancer-lineage organization and patient heterogeneity. For drugs shared between the pharmacogenomic screen and TCGA treatment records, MODAE+ predicted sensitivity was significantly associated with overall survival among patients who received each drug in 46.3% of evaluated cancer-drug pairs by log-rank testing and 41.5% by multivariable Cox analysis. Biological validation across four curated drug-gene resources identified significant expression differences exceeding 1.5-fold for 34.9-64.4% of drugs in pan-cancer analyses, based on the lowest-p-value annotated gene per drug. Drug-class-specific patterns involved intended molecular targets for targeted therapies and predominantly transport, metabolism, detoxification and resistance-related genes for classical chemotherapies. As an additional validation, we derived pretreatment responder-nonresponder gene-expression signatures from 13 external breast cancer datasets and evaluated their concordance with MODAE+ predictions across 69 signature-drug comparisons in TCGA patients treated with paclitaxel or doxorubicin. Consensus signature scores showed Spearman correlations of 0.791 with predicted paclitaxel sensitivity and 0.724 with predicted doxorubicin sensitivity, averaging 0.758 across the two drugs. Together, these complementary analyses provide supporting evidence for the clinical relevance and biological consistency of MODAE+ predictions, suggesting their potential to identify drug-sensitive tumour subgroups and generate hypotheses about mechanisms of drug resistance.

research.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine the proportion of resistance to five new and repurposed drugs (NRDs), identify risk factors for resistance, and characterize associated genetic mutations and transmission among people with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) in Shenzhen, China. METHODS: Clinical isolates were collected from all people with MDR/RR-TB admitted to Shenzhen Third People's Hospital between January 2022 and December 2024. The minimum inhibitory concentrations of five NRDs - bedaquiline (BDQ), clofazimine (CFZ), delamanid (DLM), pretomanid (PMD) and linezolid (LZD) - were determined using the broth microdilution method. Risk factors for NRD resistance were identified using Firth's penalized logistic regression. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) was performed on 99 isolates, including all NRD-resistant strains and randomly selected susceptible strains, to analyze resistance-conferring mutations, phylogeny, and clustering. RESULTS: Among 561 people with MDR/RR-TB, resistance proportions were BDQ 4.3%, CFZ 3.6%, DLM 1.1%, PMD 1.1% and LZD 1.4%. Prior NRD exposure (aOR=4.96; 95% CI, 1.95-12.61; P=0.001) and male gender (aOR=3.64; 95% CI, 1.15-11.56; P=0.028) showed strong positive associations with NRD resistance. BDQ exposure posed a higher risk of both BDQ- and CFZ-resistance than CFZ exposure. Based on the WHO mutation catalogue, WGS predicted NRD resistance with 100% specificity, sensitivity ranged from 16.7% to 75.0%. Notably, 37.5%-66.7% of resistant cases had no prior NRD exposure, and clustered isolates indicated transmitted resistance. CONCLUSION: NRD resistance among MDR/RR-TB patients in Shenzhen remains low. Although prior drug exposure is the primary risk factor, there is also evidence of transmitted resistance. NRD surveillance is essential to guide treatment and control transmission.

research.abstract: Purpose Targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) covers multiple drug resistance-associated regions, but drug-organized reports can duplicate variants across drugs and disperse a patient's variants. Through nomenclature standardization and cross-drug deduplication, we reconstructed nonredundant patient-level variant profiles and characterized multigene co-occurrence, molecular variant complexity, and reported frequency patterns. Patients and methods This single-center retrospective descriptive study included each patient's earliest eligible mutation-positive tuberculosis tNGS report from 2024-2025. The analysis dataset comprised report-derived information and did not include raw sequencing data or systematically paired phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) results. Variants were standardized using the 2023 World Health Organization catalogue, H37Rv coordinates, and Human Genome Variation Society recommendations. Duplicate patient-gene-variant records were collapsed into unique patient-variant events while retaining drug annotations. Eight mutually exclusive, exhaustive combinations were defined from RIF (rpoB), INH (katG and/or inhA), and FQ (gyrA and/or gyrB) axes. Results Fifty-seven patients contributed 180 unique patient-variant events involving nine genes and 56 standardized variants. rpoB (84.2%) and katG (64.9%) were the leading genes. The leading variants were katG p.Ser315Thr (63.2%), rpsL p.Lys43Arg (29.8%), and rpoB p.Ser450Leu (26.3%), which together accounted for 37.8% of all events; 33 of 56 variants occurred in only one patient. Seven of the eight RIF/INH/FQ combinations were observed. RIF+/INH+/FQ- was most common (31/57, 54.4%), whereas RIF+/INH+/FQ+ had the highest median numbers of genes and variants (both 5.0). Twenty-three events in 16 patients had reported frequencies below 100%, and pncA- and gyrA-associated events accounted for 60.9%. Conclusion In this mutation-positive cohort, patient-level reconstruction integrated annotations of the same variant across drugs and characterized hotspots and a long tail of variants, multigene co-occurrence within RIF/INH/FQ combinations, and report-derived frequency patterns. This traceable data structure may support laboratory report review and future genotype-phenotype studies.

research.journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
research.abstract: Abstract Bombay duck (Harpadon nehereus), once a minor by-catch in the East China Sea, has bloomed into a dominant species, altering marine ecosystems. This study explored the genomic basis of its mysterious recent success via chromosome-level genome assembly, comparative and population genomics. The genome assemblies of H. nehereus and its closely related outgroup species Saurida undosquamis were of good quality, showing a 96.7–96.8% Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologues completeness. Population resequencing supports a single panmictic population throughout the coast of China. Expanded gene families and genes under intensified and positive selection are related to osmoregulation, hypoxia tolerance, immune function and reproduction. Recent selective sweeps are mostly related to immune response. These molecular signatures are consistent with long-term adaptations to a hypoxic, polluted and fluctuating environment. These findings suggest that species genomically preadapted to environments affected by global change can suddenly become new native invaders.

research.abstract: Evaluating a 64-Species, 18-Locus Total-Evidence Supermatrix (L = 31,111 Aligned Columns; 11,436,768 Quartets), 48 Nuclear Functional CDS Orthologs, and 12 Single-Species Regional and Multi-Locus NCBI PopSet Cohorts (N = 432 Isolates) Exclusively via Constrained 100% Native Rust Bio-Suite Combinatorial Optimization (B = 1,000 UFBoot; 25,000 MCMC Generations) We reconstruct the Jurassic-to-Anthropocene global radiation, vector-host co-evolution, and historical demographic dynamics of Anopheles malaria mosquitoes across 544 verified NCBI sequence records comprising a 64-species, 18-locus supermatrix (L = 31,111 aligned columns), 48 nuclear functional coding sequences, and 12 single-species regional and multi-locus NCBI PopSet cohorts (12 × N = 36 = 432 isolates). Executed exclusively via constrained 100% Native Rust bio-suite optimization across 32 candidate RuNIE chains (total runtime 74.48 s; B = 1,000 UFBoot; 25,000 MCMC generations with 20% burn-in), RY3 purine/pyrimidine recoding under GTR+F+R4 reduces Dipteran AT-bias heterogeneity by 84.4% (RCFV = 0.0024 vs. 0.0154, ln L = -339,400.67), dating Crown Culicidae to 194.8 Ma, Crown Anophelinae to 108.4 Ma, the Gondwanan Nyssorhynchus–Cellia split to 78.9 Ma, and the African Gambiae Complex to 4.62 Ma. Native Rust quartet multispecies coalescent inference (runie-quartet-coalescent across 18 gene trees and 11,436,768 quartets in 46.97 ms) resolves 7,414,073 satisfied quartets (normalized Q = 0.6483, mean LPP = 0.8477) while ABBA-BABA tests confirm porous An. gambiae–coluzzii–arabiensis introgression (D = +0.4359 to +0.5177, Z = 12.11–13.06) and 61-state Goldman–Yang codon models identify strong purifying constraint on Orco/AgOR olfaction (ω₀ = 0.056) alongside diversifying selection on TEP1/LRIM1 immunity (ω₂ = 3.23), Anophelin/D7 saliva (ω₂ = 2.66), and VGSC/ACE1/GSTe2 resistance (ω₂ = 2.91). Finally, 12 coupled 25,000-generation Bayesian coalescent skylines reveal contrasting post-LGM savanna vs. Rift Valley expansions, Holocene agricultural/rice-paddy surges, an urban Horn of Africa An. stephensi invasion bottleneck, Amazonian BR-364 deforestation expansion, and an 89%–91% locus-specific effective population crash at the nuclear VGSC L1014F/C kdr selective-sweep locus under 21st-century pyrethroid bednet pressure while neutral mitochondrial (1Ne) and nuclear ITS2 (4Ne) demes remain demographic reservoirs. items.title: RegEvol: detection of directional selection in regulatory sequences through phenotypic predictions and phenotype-to-fitness functions
items.summary: Regulatory DNA controls when and where genes are expressed, making it a key driver of phenotypic evolution. Yet detecting selection in non-coding regions remains difficult, as most approaches rely on sequence conservation or changes in substitution rate rather than molecular effects. RegEvol bridges this gap by linking machine learning-based predictions of transcription factor binding to explicit…

research.abstract: Abstract Regulatory DNA controls when and where genes are expressed, making it a key driver of phenotypic evolution. Yet detecting selection in non-coding regions remains difficult, as most approaches rely on sequence conservation or changes in substitution rates rather than molecular effects. RegEvol bridges this gap by linking machine learning-based predictions of transcription factor binding to explicit evolutionary models. It uses the distribution of predicted mutational effects to infer fitness functions under different evolutionary scenarios including random drift, stabilising selection, and directional selection. Through maximum-likelihood estimation, it identifies the regime that best explains observed changes along a lineage from an ancestral sequence. When substitution numbers are limited, such as along short evolutionary branches, likelihood differences can be aggregated across sets of regulatory elements to increase statistical power. RegEvol corrects biases that affected previous tests based on machine learning of transcription factor binding, while remaining conservative across different levels of divergence. Applied to over 3 million Drosophila melanogaster regulatory regions, we identify 5.1% under directional selection, enriched near reproductive and immune genes. Applying the aggregation strategy to human CTCF binding across tissues reveals enrichment of directional signals in nervous and male reproductive systems. The framework is readily applicable to experimentally detected regulatory elements with alignable ancestral sequences and is adaptable to future advances in understanding regulatory function, providing a powerful basis for investigating adaptation in non-coding regions.

research.abstract: Abstract Understanding how species diversity originates, accumulates and is sustained across heterogeneous regions is a core goal of macroevolutionary and conservation biology. The genus Huperzia is an ancient and cosmopolitan lineage of lycophytes, with species widely distributed in both temperate alpine and subtropical low‐ to mid‐elevation areas, offering ideal material for investigating the diversification history of early vascular plant lineages. Here, we utilized 87 plastid genomes from 23 species to reconstruct a robust phylogenetic framework within Huperzia and found that the development of the petiole and midrib should be considered supplementary diagnostic characters in future taxonomic revisions. Our spatiotemporal and spatial phylogenetic analyses indicated that temperate and montane regions, especially northeastern China and parts of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, preserve phylogenetically distinctive paleo‐lineages, whereas subtropical evergreen broad‐leaved forests contain younger lineages associated with ecological expansion and trait differentiation. This niche transition was accompanied by repeated leaf‐trait differentiation and shifts in plastid‐gene selection in subtropical lineages, with three positively selected genes ( rps19 , chlB and atpH ) identified by branch‐site analyses. This evolutionary strategy provides a new perspective for understanding how early vascular plants maintained a dynamic equilibrium between refugial conservatism and adaptive innovation.

research.abstract: Observational studies sometimes report that individual medications are associated with lower mortality, but such signals are rarely compared across drugs and health systems. We screened prescription medications for associations with all-cause mortality using time-dependent Cox models in six cohorts from the UK, US, Finland, Hong Kong and Japan (8.93 million individuals aged 40 years or older; 1.49 billion prescriptions). Most medications were associated with higher mortality, reflecting confounding by indication. A few medications showed inverse associations with mortality, notably the varicella-zoster virus (VZV) vaccine, the antimalarials atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) and mefloquine, and the hormone replacement therapy estradiol. These associations were only modestly attenuated by adjustment for comorbidity, lifestyle and socio-economic factors, and persisted within strata defined by pre-existing disease. While adjustment for self-reported health abolished the Malarone association, probably reflecting a healthy traveler profile, the VZV association was maintained. In FinnGen, deaths from external causes, which vaccination cannot prevent, were lower among VZV vaccine users, but much less so than all-cause mortality. In a target trial emulation in All of Us, the VZV association was maintained against matched unvaccinated individuals (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.53-0.70) and pneumococcal vaccine recipients (HR 0.64, 0.55-0.74), but was attenuated against recipients of tetanus-diphtheria vaccines, a group that also has low mortality (HR 0.85, 0.70-1.03). Healthy-user selection contributes to these signals but does not appear to fully explain the VZV vaccine association, which warrants confirmation in randomized trials. This multinational atlas provides a resource for prioritizing drug-repurposing candidates in ageing research.

Using systematic manual and machine learning approaches on the choroid plexus glomus, we determined the percentages of CPECs containing thioflavin S-stained BBs as well as BB load and…

research.abstract: Human choroid plexus epithelial cells (CPECs), which produce cerebrospinal fluid and form the blood-cerebrospinal fluid barrier, accumulate discrete intracellular amyloid inclusions called Biondi bodies (BBs). Using systematic manual and machine learning approaches on the choroid plexus glomus, we determined the percentages of CPECs containing thioflavin S-stained BBs as well as BB load and spatial distributions in whole slide images from 77 cases across the human lifespan. On average, BB prevalence was near zero until age 40, rose steeply in the 5th and 6th decades, and exceeded 50% after age 70. As prevalence plateaued, BB load continued to rise with age. Accelerated BB accumulation was seen in two cases of diabetic ketoacidosis, including a 16-year-old, while an 85-year-old with the relatively rare APOE2/E2 genotype had fewer BBs than expected. BB prevalence in the choroid plexus glomus was not associated with Alzheimer's disease, but was lower in females than males. Notably, spatial clustering of BBs was universal across cases while nearest-neighbor analyses suggested cell-to-cell, prion-like BB spread that can account for the nonlinearities seen at tissue and population scales. The abrupt, nonlinear BB accumulation during midlife coincides with or precedes other common aging-associated neuropathologies of the human brain, consistent with broad BB and choroid plexus contributions to brain aging and disease.

research.abstract: Abstract Introduction Spondylodiscitis is an infectious condition involving the intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebral bodies. Although Staphylococcus aureus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis are the most common pathogens, cases caused by Gram-negative bacilli are relatively rare. Enterobacter hormaechei is an exceptionally uncommon etiologic agent in this context. Case presentation A 69-year-old Turkish male with type 2 diabetes mellitus and a history of prostate adenocarcinoma in remission, with no active immunosuppression, presented with lower back pain and elevated inflammatory markers. Initially suspected to have metastatic spinal involvement, spinal MRI revealed spondylodiscitis at the T12–L1 level. Microbiological evaluation of the needle biopsy specimen yielded Enterobacter hormaechei . Species-level identification was established by culture and MALDI-TOF MS, with off-label syndromic PCR testing (BIOFIRE ® Joint Infection Panel) providing supportive concordant results. The patient was successfully managed with surgical intervention and appropriate antimicrobial therapy. Discussion Spondylodiscitis due to Enterobacter hormaechei remains exceedingly rare. This case highlights the importance of considering atypical Gram-negative organisms in spinal infections and underscores the value of advanced microbiological methods for accurate species-level identification.

research.abstract: Abstract Background COVID-19 vaccines are highly effective at preventing severe disease and death but post-vaccination (breakthrough) infections are still seen, especially with immune-evasive variants. There is some evidence at the community level from Bangladesh. The aim of this study was to estimate prevalence, clinical profile and correlates of post-vaccination COVID-19 infection in Chandra, Kaliakair, Gazipur, Bangladesh. Methods This was a community-based cross-sectional study that included adults ≥18 years of age with at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine from March 2021 to December 2022. The respondents were 300 people who were selected by multistage sampling technique and interviewed with a pretested semi-structured questionnaire. Demographic, vaccination history, post-vaccination infection, clinical features, preventive behaviours, knowledge and comorbidities data were gathered. The chi-square test was used to test the bivariate associations and multivariable binary logistic regression was used to identify independent correlates. A p value of < 0.05 was used to determine statistical significance. Ethical Approval took from the IRB board of SCMST. Results Among 300 participants (mean age 48.0 ± 17.6 years; 52.0% male), 124 (41.3%) reported COVID-19 infection after vaccination. Of these, 24 (19.4%) were asymptomatic, 67 (54.0%) had mild disease, 24 (19.4%) had moderate disease, and 9 (7.3%) had severe disease; only 12 (9.7%) required hospitalisation. In multivariable analysis, rural residence (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 4.87; 95% CI 2.42–9.79), poor mask use (aOR 2.28; 95% CI 1.31–3.97), poor physical distancing (aOR 2.74; 95% CI 1.55–4.86), poor hand hygiene (aOR 3.61; 95% CI 2.05–6.38), and diabetes (aOR 4.46; 95% CI 1.97–10.14) were independently associated with higher odds of infection, whereas receipt of a booster dose was protective (aOR 0.23; 95% CI 0.13–0.42). Conclusion Post-vaccination infection was common but largely mild and hospitalisation was rare. The booster vaccination was protective and factors such as rural residence, poor preventive practices and diabetes were risk factors for infection. These results do reinforce the importance of booster doses coupled with ongoing preventive behaviour and targeted interventions for clinically vulnerable populations.

items.title: ECG foundation models share an age-related performance disparity that originates in the data, not the models
items.summary: BackgroundElectrocardiogram (ECG) foundation models are proposed for clinical use and promoted as fair, yet such claims are rarely tested with subgroup-stratified evaluation. We measured demographic disparities across four ECG foundation models, tested whether mitigation removes them, and asked whether the dominant disparity originates in the models or in the data and the clinical task. MethodsWe…

research.abstract: BackgroundElectrocardiogram (ECG) foundation models are proposed for clinical use and promoted as fair, yet such claims are rarely tested with subgroup-stratified evaluation. We measured demographic disparities across four ECG foundation models, tested whether mitigation removes them, and asked whether the dominant disparity originates in the models or in the data and the clinical task. MethodsWe probed frozen embeddings of four architecturally distinct ECG foundation models (ECGFounder, xECG, ECG-FM, DeepECG-SSL) in thirteen cohorts on four continents (5.4 million analysed ECGs, 31 endpoints, six held-out cohorts), stratified by age, sex and race. We examined embedding geometry, tested post-hoc correction, larger labelled training sets, comorbidity exclusion and low-rank fine-tuning, and compared each network with an untrained copy of itself and with logistic regression on classical ECG measurements. FindingsDisparities concentrated on age, not sex or race (median worst-group AUROC gap 0.028 vs 0.004 and 0.016; age exceeded sex in 97% of results) and replicated externally (ED-BWH 30-day MACE AUROC 0.81-0.90 under 40 years, 0.64-0.71 at [≥]75). Age formed a smooth gradient in the embeddings, whereas sex, though most decodable, carried no gap. No remedy closed it (low-rank adaptation: -0.007 to -0.004). Untrained copies (r=0.81, 102 pairs) and classical measurements ({rho}=0.90) reproduced the endpoint-specific gaps, and pretraining raised AUROC (+0.067) without changing them. The largest race effect, higher potassium error in Black patients, vanished at matched true potassium. InterpretationECG foundation models carry an age-structured disparity that replicates externally and survives mitigation. Because untrained networks and a classical model reproduce it, the results indicate that it is inherited from the age structure of the ECG and its labels rather than created by the models, so switching or adapting models will not remove it. Age-stratified reporting, untrained and classical baselines, and age-specific thresholds and recalibration are therefore needed. FundingAustrian Research Promotion Agency (FFG; CARDISENSE project, grant FO999922422). Graphical abstract O_FIG O_LINKSMALLFIG WIDTH=200 HEIGHT=70 SRC="FIGDIR/small/26366943v1_ufig1.gif" ALT="Figure 1"> View larger version (23K): [email removed]@[email removed]@17e649_HPS_FORMAT_FIGEXP M_FIG C_FIG Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed, Google Scholar, and arXiv from database inception to October, 2026, using combinations of the terms "ECG" or "electrocardiogram", "foundation model" or "self-supervised", and "fairness", "bias", "equity", "subgroup", or "demographic", with no language restriction. Open-weight ECG foundation models have proliferated and are increasingly proposed for clinical use, and benchmarks compare them on aggregate accuracy without stratifying by subgroup. The fairness literature documents demographic performance gaps in task-specific ECG classifiers, most often for sex or race on single tasks in single cohorts, and the remedies it proposes act on the model (reweighting, adversarial debiasing, group-robust training, fine-tuning). The one subgroup analysis of ECG foundation models we found covered two models of one family on their own endpoints, stratified by age and sex only. To our knowledge, no study has evaluated several architecturally distinct ECG foundation models along age, sex and race across endpoint families and continents, and none has tested whether a disparity found in a foundation model is also present without any pretraining or without deep learning. Added value of this studyEvaluating four architecturally distinct ECG foundation models across thirteen cohorts on four continents, including six held-out external cohorts, we show that strong average and external discrimination coexists with a disparity that concentrates on age, not sex or race, and that replicates externally. The pattern has a consistent substrate: age is encoded as a smooth gradient in the embeddings, while sex and race, both decodable, carry no comparable gap. The gap is shared across every architecture and pretraining objective, and neither post-hoc correction, larger labelled training sets, exclusion of comorbid ECGs nor low-rank fine-tuning closes it. Two controls explain why: untrained copies of the same networks and a logistic regression on classical ECG measurements reproduce the endpoint-specific age gaps, which indicates that the gap is inherited from the data and the clinical task rather than learned in pretraining. Implications of all the available evidenceFairness evaluation of ECG foundation models should prioritise age and report age-stratified performance as a primary result, because a threshold fixed on the pooled population operates at a worse point for older patients than the headline metric implies. Because the gap persists across architectures, vendors, fine-tuning and even untrained networks, switching models will not resolve it. Evaluations should include an untrained and a classical baseline before attributing a gap to a model, and services deploying these models should use age-specific thresholds and recalibration, or at minimum report and monitor performance by age band.

ObjectiveTo develop and internally evaluate an electronic health record (EHR)-based machine-learning model to identify patients more likely to receive a documented cardiac arrhythmia diagnosis. MethodsWe retrospectively evaluated EHR data (2018-2025)…

research.abstract: Background Cardiac arrhythmias may remain unrecognized in adults with chronic disease. Established risk scores primarily address atrial fibrillation. Objective To develop and internally evaluate an electronic health record (EHR)–based machine-learning model to identify patients more likely to receive a documented cardiac arrhythmia diagnosis. Methods We retrospectively evaluated EHR data (2018–2025) from one healthcare organization among adults with type 2 diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic kidney disease, or coronary artery disease. Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost were compared. XGBoost was selected using internal validation, reduced to 30 features using Shapley additive explanations, and evaluated in a holdout set with data ending one day before the index date. Sensitivity analyses excluded information recorded within 30, 90, or 180 days before the index date. An atrial fibrillation/flutter-specific analysis compared XGBoost with CHARGE-AF and HARMS 2 -AF. Results Among 30,356 patients, 6,835 (22.5%) had a qualifying arrhythmia diagnosis. In 3,051 holdout patients, XGBoost achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.894 (95% CI 0.879–0.908) and an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.792 (95% CI 0.763–0.822). At a 0.5 threshold, sensitivity was 0.564, specificity 0.971, and precision 0.857. AUROC remained 0.896–0.897 across earlier cutoffs. In the common score-calculable atrial fibrillation/flutter subset ( n = 2,436), AUROCs were 0.883 for XGBoost, 0.712 for CHARGE-AF, and 0.554 for HARMS 2 -AF. Conclusions XGBoost demonstrated strong internal discrimination for documented arrhythmias. External validation and prospective evaluation are needed to assess generalizability and clinical utility.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Cardiorenal syndrome (CRS) is associated with poor outcomes. Risk factors for progressive CRS are not understood in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Objectives This study aimed to determine the incidence of progressive CRS and risk factors in individuals with CKD. Methods Adults with CKD in the Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC) study excluding those with heart failure (HF) at baseline were included (n = 3,557). We defined progressive CRS as developing HF and end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) within 12 months. ESKD was defined as needing renal replacement therapy or renal transplant. The associations of baseline risk factors with progressive CRS were examined using Cox proportional hazards models. A sensitivity analysis assessed risk factors in those who developed HF before ESKD and vice versa. Results 161 patients (4.5%) developed progressive CRS. Traditional risk factors [multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios (HR) (95% CI)] associated with progressive CRS in multivariable models included lower education [1.90 (1.28,2.83)], cardiovascular disease [1.53 (1.07,2.18)], lower estimated glomerular filtration rate [0.64 (0.51,0.82)] and higher albumin to creatinine ratio [2.44 (1.98,3.02)]. Novel risk factors associated included higher levels of alkaline phosphatase, brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF-15), hemoglobin A1C, and lower hemoglobin. Risk factors associated with both ESKD before HF and HF before ESKD were kidney dysfunction, albuminuria, and mineral bone disorder (higher alkaline phosphatase and PTH), inflammation (TNF-α), fibrotic factor (GDF-15), and anemia. Diabetes, CVD, systolic blood pressure, waist circumference, HbA1c, and BNP were more strongly associated when HF preceded ESKD. Conclusions Both traditional risk factors and novel risk factors associated with inflammation, mineral bone disorder, anemia, diabetes control, albuminuria, worse kidney function, and fibrotic factors are associated with progressive CRS in individuals with CKD. Many of these risk factors are modifiable representing potential areas for intervention.

research.abstract: Abstract Introduction Problematic gambling is an increasing public health concern that also affects U.S. Veterans. Problematic gambling in Veterans correlates with several other factors, including socio-economic issues like homelessness and legal problems, and mental health issues like post-traumatic stress disorder, and suicide attempt. Our objective was to analyze differences between U.S. Veterans experiencing problematic gambling compared to similar U.S. Veterans who did not, according to diagnostic codes. Materials and Methods Electronic health records from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) for health care encounters between 2016-01-01 and 2024-12-31 served as data for this study. We performed a one-to-one match on age, race, ethnicity, gender, and VA station for 775 Veterans diagnosed with problematic gambling by International Classification of Diseases 10 th edition codes, to Veterans not receiving one of the diagnostic codes relevant to gambling. We then compared comorbidity diagnoses, marital status, and VA care encounters, applying chi-squared and t-test analyses. Results There were many statistically significant differences in care use, marital status, and comorbidities. Veterans with problematic gambling were more likely to experience other substance abuse, including opioid use disorder (22.5% vs 8.4%) and alcohol use disorder (56.3% vs 25.9%). Veterans with problematic gambling were also more likely to experience mental illness, including major depressive disorder (64.9% vs 46.7%), post-traumatic stress disorder (50.8% vs 43.1%), and suicide attempt (5.3% vs 3.0%), and socio-economic issues, including economic hardship (28.7% vs 16.3%), homelessness (33.9% vs 14.8%), legal problems (13.4% vs 6.8%) and social/family problems (53.6% vs 46.5%). Veterans experiencing problematic gambling also were less likely to be married and received more VA outpatient care. Conclusions The findings suggest that problematic gambling in Veterans correlates with worse outcomes when comparing similar Veterans receiving care through the same facilities. It is feasible to screen for problematic gambling in primary care encounters, however the extent of screening in VA care is unknown. Screening for problematic gambling in VA primary care may enable providers to assist patients experiencing problematic gambling to find directed care.

research.abstract: Background Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global infectious disease, and novel host-derived biomarkers are needed to improve diagnosis. Circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) are promising biomarkers due to their stability and immune regulatory functions; however, clinically validated TB-associated miRNAs remain limited. This study aimed to identify circulating miRNAs associated with active pulmonary TB. Methods This study included 90 participants: active pulmonary TB (n=30), cured TB (n=30), and healthy controls (n=30). Candidate miRNAs were screened by pooled plasma miRNA profiling and further examined using three publicly available miRNA datasets. Circulating miR-26b-5p was quantified by RT-qPCR. Associations with active TB status were assessed using logistic regression, and discriminatory performance was evaluated by ROC analysis. Putative miR-26b-5p target genes and enriched pathways were explored using bioinformatic analyses. Results Microarray screening identified 108 candidate miRNAs, and cross-dataset analysis identified miR-26b-5p as the only overlapping candidate with consistent downregulation. Circulating miR-26b-5p was lower in active TB and higher in the clinically cured group. It remained associated with active-TB status after adjustment for BMI and PLR. miR-26b-5p showed an AUC of 0.867, while the combined model achieved an AUC of 0.956. Bioinformatic analysis identified 74 putative genes, with EP300, GSK3B, and PTEN as network hubs and PI3K-Akt among the enriched pathways. Conclusion Circulating miR-26b-5p was associated with active pulmonary TB and showed preliminary discriminatory value, supporting its further evaluation as a candidate host-response marker.

items.title: Genomic characterization and evolutionary path of human satellite 1B in primates highlight a dynamic relationship with transposable elements
items.summary: Human Satellite 1B (HSat1B) remains one of the least characterized classical human satellite DNAs, despite its massive abundance on the human Y chromosome. Its tripartite ~2.5 kb monomer - comprising an AluY fragment, a GC-rich unit (here named H1B) and an AT-rich block - points to an evolutionary origin tightly linked to transposable elements (TEs). research.abstract: Abstract Human Satellite 1B (HSat1B) remains one of the least characterized classical human satellite DNAs, despite its massive abundance on the human Y chromosome. Its tripartite ∼2.5 kb monomer - comprising an AluY fragment, a GC-rich unit (here named H1B) and an AT-rich block - points to an evolutionary origin tightly linked to transposable elements (TEs). Here, we present the first comprehensive comparative genomic, phylogenetic, and transcriptional characterization of HSat1B across 10 primate species using Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) and chromosome-scale long-read assemblies, combined with DNA-FISH, RNA-FISH and long-read transcriptomic analyses. We demonstrate that while canonical tandem HSat1B arrays are restricted to Homininae (human, chimpanzee, bonobo, and gorilla), the core H1B unit and its structural variants (H1Bsv1 and H1Bsv2) occur across all 10 primate genomes, including strepsirrhines (lemur). This indicates that the H1B sequence predates the assembly of the composite HSat1B monomer by at least 60 million years. H1B variants consistently map within TE-rich genomic contexts, supporting a stepwise, TE-mediated model of satellite diversification and mobilization. Within Homininae, humans exhibit a dramatic lineage-specific expansion driven by Yq12 amplification (∼14.2 Mb; 92% of total genomic content), whereas non-human great apes carry smaller, highly polymorphic autosomal and Y-linked arrays. Finally, we show that H1B-containing sequences are transcriptionally active in human and gorilla nuclei via RNA-FISH and characterize heterogeneous H1B/ Alu chimeric non-coding transcripts in the human male germline. Collectively, our findings uncover the birth and Homininae-specific expansion of a composite satellite DNA seeded by an ancient primate sequence module and sculpted by transposable elements.

items.summary: Transposable elements (TEs) are major drivers of genomic diversity, yet understanding their mobility and functional impact requires their accurate description in genomes.
