Hence, TE annotation with a library from a single reference misses families absent…

research.abstract: Abstract Transposable elements (TEs) are major drivers of genomic diversity, yet understanding their mobility and functional impact requires their accurate description in genomes. TE annotation is still typically performed genome-by-genome. TEs are often shared between some members of the same or closely related species. Hence, TE annotation with a library from a single reference misses families absent from that assembly, whereas building independent per-genome libraries fails to consistently surface shared TEs, hindering comparison. Here, we present Earl Grey ParTEA, a fully automated Snakemake pipeline extending the functionality of Earl Grey for comparative TE annotation across genome panels. ParTEA builds a single non-redundant TE library from all input genomes, resolves chimeric consensus sequences, and uses this shared library to annotate every genome, enabling direct comparison of TE family diversity, abundance, shared and private content, and activity landscapes. Optional modules provide TE library saturation analysis, BUSCO-based assembly quality control, and phylogenetic ordering of outputs. We applied ParTEA to sets of genomes spanning evolutionary scales: ten Arabidopsis thaliana accessions, ten Drosophila species, and ten species spanning the fungal kingdom. The Drosophila TE library expanded from 343 to 1,852 curated families including a previously missed rolling circle element with over 6,000 copies in D. miranda . The proportion of TE families shared across all genomes was highest within A. thaliana (97.3%), 37.7% across Drosophila species and only 0.5% across the set of fungi. ParTEA is available through Bioconda and represents a computationally efficient reproducible framework for comparative TE analysis in the era of large-scale genome analyses.

items.title: HiSpoT: a novel one-tube dual-barcode PCR method for NGS spoligotyping amplicon library preparation in Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex
items.summary: Tuberculosis remains one of the leading infectious causes of death globally, making rapid, accurate, and affordable strain typing essential for effective outbreak tracking and epidemiological surveillance. To address the limitations and high costs of current typing methods, we developed a novel one-tube, dual-barcode PCR method for preparing targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) amplicon…

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Tuberculosis remains one of the leading infectious causes of death globally, making rapid, accurate, and affordable strain typing essential for effective outbreak tracking and epidemiological surveillance. To address the limitations and high costs of current typing methods, we developed a novel one-tube, dual-barcode PCR method for preparing targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) amplicon libraries for spoligotyping of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC), which we termed HiSpoT (High-throughput Spoligotyping by Targeted next generation sequencing). The assay targets 43 conserved spacer oligonucleotides in the CRISPR direct repeat (DR) region and is presented here together with the previously unpublished, difficult-to-design dual-barcode primer set needed to multiplex 96 samples in a single tube. HiSpoT is accurate, fast, high-throughput, and low-cost, eliminating the need for a commercial NGS library preparation kit. Because HiSpoT is PCR-based, the resulting spoligotypes remain directly comparable with the large PCR-based spoligotype databases accumulated over decades, enabling rapid outbreak tracking and biogeographic characterization of a country’s tuberculosis burden while higher-resolution whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data are obtained. Analysis of 288 clinical MTBC isolates from Israel (2020-2022) demonstrated a broad range of genetic lineages, and comparison of 79 isolates analyzed by both HiSpoT and WGS showed 70% full concordance, with essentially all discrepancies attributable to single-spacer insertion-element disruptions of PCR primer sites. We also present two open-source Google Colab Python tools, Spoligotyping_MTBC_gcl and its condensed HiSpoT_Spoligotyping_v8_ready VIBE variant, freely available on GitHub, which automatically process Illumina paired-end fastq output from HiSpoT or WGS and report binary and octal spoligotypes, spoligo international types (SIT), and MTBC family assignments with accompanying quality-control reports. IMPORTANCE Tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis , is the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent worldwide, and rapid, accurate, and affordable strain typing is essential for tracking outbreaks and directing limited public health resources. The decades-old laboratory method for spoligotyping, a widely used genetic fingerprint for this bacterium, is slow, labor-intensive, and hard to read. Newer sequencing-based approaches solve these problems but usually still need an expensive, time-consuming commercial kit to prepare samples for sequencing. This work describes HiSpoT, a simplified, low-cost, one-tube method that prepares samples for sequencing without a commercial kit, cutting turnaround from about a week to about two days while testing many samples together. Because HiSpoT results agree with results obtained from older typing methods, laboratories anywhere with basic sequencing equipment can compare results to decades of stored international data. Two free, open-source computer programs are also provided so laboratories with limited bioinformatics expertise can analyze their sequencing data automatically.

items.title: Do divergent mitochondrial backgrounds alter the fate of nuclear alleles during hybridization and admixture?
items.summary: Hybridization brings together genetic variation from different populations or species into admixed genomes. As selection sorts this variation, the fate of each allele is determined by its fitness effect in the new hybrid genomic background. Because mitochondrial genes coevolve with the nuclear genome, they may be especially sensitive to foreign nuclear backgrounds, making them potential…

research.abstract: Abstract Hybridization brings together genetic variation from different populations or species into admixed genomes. As selection sorts this variation, the fate of each allele is determined by its fitness effect in the new hybrid genomic background. Because mitochondrial genes coevolve with the nuclear genome, they may be especially sensitive to foreign nuclear backgrounds, making them potential “hot-spots” for hybrid incompatibilities. Here, we test whether selection against mitonuclear incompatibilities drives repeatable hybridization outcomes. Specifically, we experimentally evolved three sets of five populations of hybrid Drosophila melanogaster , each carrying the same nuclear chromosomes but paired with one of three increasingly divergent mitochondrial DNA backgrounds. We hypothesized that accumulated incompatibilities would result in different patterns of nuclear admixture among mitochondrial backgrounds. To test this, we tracked nuclear allele frequencies in all 15 populations by whole-genome sequencing at intermediate time points. After 25 generations, we observed that rapid genomic evolution produced a strikingly parallel mosaic of both nuclear ancestries, independent of mitochondrial background. Contrary to our hypothesis, we found no evidence that mitochondrial background shaped nuclear admixture, even for interspecific combinations. These results suggest that in species with large effective population sizes, efficient purifying selection limits the accumulation of mitonuclear incompatibilities, allowing selection on nuclear alleles to promote repeatable ancestry sorting immediately following hybridization.

We developed and evaluated a streamlined symmetric POCUS protocol for pulmonary TB in a high-burden setting. research.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is a low-cost, radiation-free triage tool but lacks standardized acquisition protocols for tuberculosis (TB). We developed and evaluated a streamlined symmetric POCUS protocol for pulmonary TB in a high-burden setting. Methods Ugandan participants aged ≥13 years with confirmed pulmonary TB, household TB exposure, or a non-TB respiratory condition underwent an 18-position POCUS examination (12 lung zones and 6 pre-established extrapulmonary positions). Random Forest classifiers using prespecified pathologic features were developed in a fixed stratified 75/25 training/holdout split. All symmetric 2-, 4-, and 6-zone combinations were evaluated in training data. The best protocol of each size was locked and tested in the holdout set. Results Among 318 analyzed participants, 118 (37.1%) had pulmonary TB and 200 were TB-negative, including 102 with other respiratory conditions (ORC). The model-selected 6-zone protocol comprised bilateral anterior-superior, lateral-superior, and posterior-superior lung zones. For TB versus all TB-negative participants, the AUCs for the 6-zone, 12-zone, and 18-position protocols were 0.82 (95% CI, 0.73-0.92), 0.81 (0.70–0.92), and 0.81 (0.71–0.91), respectively (all P > 0.76). For TB versus ORC, AUCs were 0.81 (0.70–0.91), 0.85 (0.76–0.93), and 0.85 (0.76–0.94), respectively (all P > 0.45). The 2-zone protocol had a lower AUC than the 6-zone protocol for TB versus all TB-negative participants ( P = 0.004). Shred sign, consolidation, and B-lines with irregular pleura were the strongest TB-associated findings. Conclusions A fixed 6-zone lung POCUS examination showed similar discrimination for TB to more comprehensive 12-lung-zone and 18-position protocols. This supports a simpler, scalable approach to TB triage.

items.title: Unraveling the genetic architecture of the human mammillary bodies
items.summary: The mammillary bodies are a central component of the hippocampal-diencephalic-cingulate network that is critically involved in emotion processing and memory function, yet their genetic architecture remains unknown. We conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) of mammillary body volume in 38,064 participants from the UK Biobank and replicated our findings in the Rhineland Study cohort (N =…

research.abstract: ABSTRACT The mammillary bodies are a central component of the hippocampal–diencephalic-cingulate network that is critically involved in emotion processing and memory function, yet their genetic architecture remains unknown. We conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) of mammillary body volume in 38,064 participants from the UK Biobank and replicated our findings in the Rhineland Study cohort (N = 4,860). Mammillary body and hypothalamic subregional volumes were derived from structural brain MRIs using FastSurfer-HypVINN, an established and validated deep learning-based segmentation tool. Univariate GWAS identified 34 genomic loci associated with mammillary body volume, including 26 novel loci, with 20 loci showing replication in the Rhineland Study. Meta-analysis across both cohorts (N = 42,924) identified 44 associated loci, of which 35 were novel. Multivariate GWAS of hypothalamic subregions identified 55 loci, including 40 novel associations. Integrative cross-omics analyses identified MEI1 and CAPZA1 as key molecular candidates, with genetically regulated MEI1 expression and circulating CAPZA1 protein levels partially mediating genetic effects on mammillary body volume. Genetic correlation and Mendelian randomization analyses further revealed a bidirectional relationship between mammillary body volume and major depressive disorder. Together, our findings elucidate the genetic architecture of mammillary body volume and its relation to mental disorders.

This systematic review and meta-analysis estimated pooled proportions of treatment success, mortality, treatment failure and loss to follow-up (LTFU) among TB patients in Cameroon, and identified predictors of unfavorable…

research.abstract: BackgroundTuberculosis (TB) remains a major public health challenge in Cameroon, yet national evidence on treatment outcomes across the full spectrum of routine care is limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis estimated pooled proportions of treatment success, mortality, treatment failure and loss to follow-up (LTFU) among TB patients in Cameroon, and identified predictors of unfavorable outcomes. MethodsPubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, African Journals Online and the Cochrane Library were searched, supplemented by Google Scholar and reference-list screening. Observational studies conducted in Cameroon reporting at least one WHO-defined treatment outcome were eligible. Pooled proportions and adjusted odds ratios (AOR) were estimated with random-effects models meta-analysis. Data were analyzed using R Statistics version 4.6.1. ResultsThirty-two studies (25 cohorts, 7 cross-sectional), conducted between 1998 and 2022 across six of Cameroons ten regions, were included. Pooled treatment success was 78.2% (95% CI: 73.8-82.1; 27 reports; 71,784 participants; I{superscript 2} = 98.2%), mortality 8.1% (95% CI: 5.5-11.7; 25 reports; 71,870 participants; I{superscript 2} = 97.8%), treatment failure 0.9% (95% CI: 0.5-1.4; 26 reports; 71,389 participants; I{superscript 2} = 89.1%) and LTFU 6.8% (95% CI: 5.0-9.1; 26 reports; 70,768 participants; I{superscript 2} = 98.6%). Mortality was highest in the South-West (16.2%) and among TB/HIV-coinfected patients (30.5%), and lowest among children (5.0%). Treatment success was lowest in the Littoral (71.1%) and among TB/HIV-coinfected patients (60.8%) and highest among multidrug-resistant TB (89.3%) and pediatric patients (86.8%). Treatment failure significantly declined from 2.9% before 2005 to 0.5% from 2020 onward (p < 0.001). Significant predictors of unfavorable outcomes were HIV positivity (AOR = 2.57; 95% CI: 1.86-3.55), previous TB treatment (AOR = 1.99; 95% CI: 1.40-2.84), male sex (AOR = 1.67; 95% CI: 1.45-1.92), age [≤]40 years (AOR = 1.45; 95% CI: 1.06-1.98) and absence of antiretroviral therapy (AOR = 1.71; 95% CI: 1.15-2.54). ConclusionsTB treatment outcomes in Cameroon remain suboptimal, with nearly one in five patients not achieving treatment success and high mortality among TB/HIV-coinfected individuals. Strengthening TB/HIV service integration, early antiretroviral therapy initiation, targeted support for previously treated patients and men, and improved retention in care are needed. Systematic review registration numberCRD420261404490

Hence, we estimated the prevalence of HIV/TB coinfection and treatment outcomes in Cameroon…

research.abstract: BackgroundHuman immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and tuberculosis (TB) form one of the deadliest syndemics, and sub-Saharan Africa bears over 80% of HIV-associated TB deaths. In Cameroon, evidence on HIV/TB coinfection remains unsynthesized across regions and populations, obscuring the national burden. Hence, we estimated the prevalence of HIV/TB coinfection and treatment outcomes in Cameroon. MethodsFollowing PRISMA 2020 (PROSPERO: CRD420261399169), we searched PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, African Journals Online, and grey literature for English- and French-language studies conducted in Cameroon. Reports were independently screened, their data extracted, and their methodology appraised using Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Random-effects models pooled prevalence, treatment outcomes, and adjusted odds ratios. Heterogeneity was assessed with I{superscript 2}. ResultsSeventy studies (1995-2023) were included, 87.1% at low risk of bias. Pooled HIV prevalence among TB patients was 29.2% (95% CI: 26.3-32.3; 67 studies; n=57,169; I{superscript 2} = 97.8%), with no significant evidence of publication bias. Prevalence was higher from 2007 onwards (29.9%; 62 studies; n=55,358) than before (20.5%; 5 studies; n=1,811). It was highest in the North-West (41.9%; 7 studies; n=6,324) versus Littoral (25.0%; 15 studies; n=10,419) and West (23.8%; 6 studies; n=4,206); and in extrapulmonary TB (42.3%; 3 studies; n=371) versus mixed forms (37.7%; 21 studies; n=37,239) and pulmonary TB (23.9%; 37 studies; n=16,096) (all p<0.05). Among coinfected patients, pooled treatment success was 75.9% (95% CI: 70.4-80.8; 8 studies; n=4,230), mortality 21.1% (95% CI: 11.9-34.7; 10 studies; n=4,403), loss to follow-up 7.7% (95% CI: 4.3-13.3; 5 studies; n=3,103), and treatment failure 0.3% (95% CI: 0.1-1.5; 6 studies; n=3,520). Lack of antiretroviral therapy (ART) increased the odds of unfavorable outcomes (AOR = 1.90; 95% CI: 1.15-3.12; 2 studies). ConclusionsApproximately three in ten TB patients in Cameroon are coinfected with HIV, with marked regional and clinical variation. Treatment success remains below national targets. Strengthening TB-HIV service integration, routine HIV testing, and timely ART initiation and continuation is essential to reduce the HIV-associated TB morbidity and mortality in the country.

research.abstract: Abstract Sugar beet (Beta vulgaris ssp. vulgaris) is a major global source of sucrose. Domestication and a history of breeding have shaped the distribution of deleterious mutations across the genome. Accurately resolving these variants offers a compelling avenue to accelerate crop improvement through breeding or genetic engineering. We combine three evolutionary methods to identify putatively deleterious derived mutations: angiosperm-wide DNA language deep learning model (PlantCaduceus), fine-scale evolutionary rates from Amaranthaceae plant family sequence alignments using PAML and PhyloP. We defined a high-confidence set of ∼5k deleterious variants enriched for alleles under negative selection. We then evaluate these deleterious mutations across a multi-study panel of more than 1,900 whole-genome sequenced wild and cultivated beet accessions. We found that domesticated beet accessions exhibit higher deleterious load relative to wild maritima, yet sugar beet carries significantly fewer deleterious variants than other cultivated beet crops. Historical trends show a decline in genetic load across more than a century of sugar beet entries in the US NPGS, likely reflecting sustained purging during modern breeding. This combinatorial method of leveraging evolutionary conservation reveals how deleterious mutations have shaped sugar beet breeding history and provides potential targets for future selection, causal-variant discovery, and precision genome engineering.

For antagonistic fungi, specialization often involves acquiring genes for novel secretions-including proteins and specialized metabolites-that mediate nutrient acquisition and host defense interactions. Here, we conducted a phylogenomic investigation of Sympodiorosea, ascomycetes…

research.abstract: Abstract Biological interactions involving host-associated fungi are driven by chemistry shaped over evolutionary time. For antagonistic fungi, specialization often involves acquiring genes for novel secretions—including proteins and specialized metabolites—that mediate nutrient acquisition and host defense interactions. Here, we conducted a phylogenomic investigation of Sympodiorosea, ascomycetes commonly found in basal fungus-growing ant gardens. While Sympodiorosea and related genera (Escovopsis, Luteomyces, Manidigitorum, Escovopsioides) are canonically viewed as virulent mycoparasites, non-virulent species may also emerge within these attine-associated fungi. We explored genomic variation in Sympodiorosea to assess potential alternative lifestyles, focusing on the diversity and evolution of metabolic genes. Our study revealed a constrained selective landscape across the Sympodiorosea genome. However, outcomes of in vitro host interactions were diverse and predictable based on the antagonist's ant-species-of-origin, suggesting functional diversification. Phylogenomics indicated that gene gain/loss events in carbohydrate-active enzymes and specialized metabolism drive this diversification. Although selection acts intensely on metabolism-related genes overall, specific metabolic genes experience diversifying selection, indicating their critical role in host associations. Furthermore, Sympodiorosea exhibits protease gene expansions and contractions discordant with a strictly mycoparasitic lifestyle, suggesting either an alternative lifestyle within ant gardens or recent evolution from other niches. These results provide novel insights into fungal genome evolution and the chemistry of the fungus-growing ant symbiosis.

items.title: BEAGLE 4.1: A high-performance library for computation on phylogenetic trees across diverse parallel architectures
items.summary: Efficient evaluation of sequence data likelihoods and their high-dimensional gradients on phylogenetic trees improves inference under both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian frameworks. Here, we present BEAGLE 4.1, a high-performance library for statistical phylogenetics that incorporates new algorithms to evaluate these gradients on phylogenetic trees. We also provide new hardware implementations…

research.abstract: Efficient evaluation of sequence data likelihoods and their high-dimensional gradients on phylogenetic trees improves inference under both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian frameworks. Here, we present BEAGLE 4.1, a high-performance library for statistical phylogenetics that incorporates new algorithms to evaluate these gradients on phylogenetic trees. We also provide new hardware implementations for both likelihoods and gradients supporting ARM NEON intrinsics and optimized matrix multiplication units -- called tensor cores -- on NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs). We benchmark the performance scaling of the library across a number of patterns and taxa on multi-core CPUs and GPUs, and compare the speedup afforded by NVIDIA and AMD GPUs as well as performance scaling with an increasing number of GPUs. We show that multi-core CPU implementations provide up to a fourfold speedup over single-threaded CPU implementations and up to an tenfold speedup for nucleotide and codon models, respectively, with performance generally improving as the number of taxa and site patterns increases. GPUs outperform multi-threaded CPU implementations for a realistic number of patterns, even for nucleotide models with a small state-space size of 4, while for codon models they provide substantially higher performance gains even for a single pattern or four taxa. Tensor cores on GPUs provide up to 2-fold speedup relative to standard CUDA cores for codon models. Using NEON instructions on ARM CPUs affords up to a $\sim 1.3$-fold speedup over non-SIMD implementation with the speedup going down to 1.1-fold at 8 CPU threads. We provide these new algorithms to evaluate the gradient and efficient hardware implementations for both likelihood and gradient calculations through BEAGLE 4.1, such that they can be readily integrated into phylogenetic software packages.

research.abstract: In 2023, an estimated 13% of worldwide deaths resulting from antimicrobial resistance (AMR) were due to drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). The World Health Organization (WHO) documented a dramatic, sixfold increase in the number of patients treated with 6-month all-oral (BPaLM) regimens, from 5,653 patients in 2023, to 34,000 patients by 2024, while also documenting an emergence of bedaquiline resistance in real-world cohorts and a lack of efficacy of BCG revaccination in the BCG-PRIME Phase 2b trial against sustained Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Concurrently, the M72/AS01E subunit vaccine trial completed recruitment (approximately 20,000 individuals) across five high-burden countries, 11 months ahead of scheduled completion date. The first randomized controlled trial assessing DRTB-HDT host-directed therapy for DR-TB in adults (metformin + dovramilast), conducted at five international sites, is entering the late-stage readout phase. This synthesis of data, covering the period from 2015 through 2026, across six different dimensions includes molecular mechanisms of resistance, novel antimicrobial treatment modalities, host-directed therapy, immunity associated with regulatory compliance, adjuvants to vaccines, and the clinical translation of vaccine candidates. The Molecular-to-Translational continuum is used as a framework for the synthesis, with the regulatory immune function domain (T regulatory cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and check-point axes) linking all five domains. Our central hypothesis is that drug resistance evolution of the microbe and failure of the host to maintain regulatory immunity are interdependent and create a bidirectional relationship with each other. We have identified nine major research gaps, with milestone dates from 2026 to 2030, based on unresolved controversies regarding the bedaquiline resistance catalog and the acquisition versus transmission narrative.

items.summary: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on…

research.abstract: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Targeted diagnostics such as culturing, antigen assays, and multiplex PCR panels identify only predefined organisms and can fail to identify atypical or novel infections. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on mutable reference databases, and high computational cost. To combat these challenges, we introduce MicrobeRT, an integrated suite of genomic language models fine-tuned to classify metagenomic sequencing reads across three tasks: (i) species level taxonomic identification, (ii) antibiotic resistance gene detection, and (iii) pathogenicity assessment. The framework builds on three pre-trained genomic language models - Nucleotide Transformer (Dalla-Torre et al 2025), DNABERT (Ji et al 2021, Zhou et al 2024), and HyenaDNA (Nguyen et al 2024) - leveraging their large-scale genomic pre-training, adaptability to downstream tasks, and, in the case of HyenaDNA, ability to capture long-range sequence dependencies. The models are fine-tuned on large, curated datasets spanning microbial, viral, fungal, and human genomes, including more than 500,000 genomes and 250,000 antibiotic resistance gene sequences. To evaluate the performance of our fine-tuned genomic language models across classification tasks, we developed a benchmarking framework that compares MicrobeRT against state-of-the-art (SOTA) bioinformatics tools. Across both simulated and empirical datasets, the models achieve strong performance while reducing computational overhead. MicrobeRT is released as open-source software, enabling further fine-tuning and reproducible integration of alternative models and classifiers. We also demonstrate seamless, drop-in integration by incorporating our fine-tuned taxonomic classification models as an optional add-on within the open-source TaxTriage pipeline (Merritt et al 2026). MicrobeRT demonstrates the feasibility of three clinically relevant multi-label analyses, offering a practical path to scalable, reproducible metagenomic diagnostics and enabling broader deployment of AI/ML-enhanced infectious disease testing.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT West Nile virus (WNV) is a flavivirus whose cycle involves mosquitoes and avian hosts that occasionally may infect horses and humans as “dead‐end hosts.” Human infection is mostly asymptomatic, sometimes leading to febrile or neuroinvasive disease. In 2025, Italy experienced its largest epidemic with an unprecedented geographic spread (79 provinces; 52% of cases in central Italy). Here we report whole‑genome sequencing and phylogeographic analysis of 39 WNV lineage 2 samples collected in Lazio and Campania regions between July and September 2025 from humans and animal samples. All 2025 strains belonged to a Southern Italian clade that diversified around 2020, with evidence of earlier circulation in 2024. All the 2025 genomes shared a substitution that lies in envelope protein domain III (K399R), potentially influencing interactions with the viral membrane. The same mutation was previously detected in Eastern European strains, leading to the hypothesis of introductions in Italy via migratory birds from these regions. Phylogeography identified strong viral dispersal routes within Central Italy supporting a pattern of short‑range spread and local overwintering. Overall, results highlight the roles of ecological conditions and cross‑border transmission dynamics in shaping the 2025 Italian epidemic, underscoring the need for integrated genomic/ecological surveillance.

research.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) results from acquiring mutations or genes that allow microbes to withstand antimicrobials. These genetic modifications can also cause non-selected changes in other cell phenotypes, such as fitness and susceptibility to antibiotic classes different from the one under selection. These collateral effects of AMR acquisition could be exploited to improve treatments. This is increasingly important in light of AMR as a major global health problem, associated with 4.71 million deaths worldwide in 2021, with 1.14 million deaths directly attributable to AMR. Additionally, the lack of development of novel antimicrobials active against resistant infections continues to compound the crisis. Even if new antimicrobials are developed, resistance will most likely emerge through adaptive evolution. Therefore, it is imperative to explore strategies to maintain the efficacy of new and existing antibiotics and limit the acquisition of AMR to continue to treat infections successfully. Understanding the impact of resistance acquisition on the bacterial phenotype, including collateral effects, has the potential to improve therapeutic outcomes. In this perspective, we will summarize the collateral effects of resistance acquisition, including fitness costs, collateral susceptibility networks, mutant selection windows and the probability of establishment of bacterial populations, and explore how these may be exploited to enhance the effectiveness of existing antibiotics. We will also discuss how challenges such as genetic background, polymicrobial infections and the environment are current barriers to the translation of these principles into the clinic.

research.abstract: 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across 64 species and 18 loci (L = 26,700 aligned columns; Lagomorpha outgroups, Sciuromorpha, Castorimorpha, Dipodoidea, invasive Muridae, and New World Cricetidae: Arvicolinae, Neotominae, and Sigmodontinae) coupled with 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) single-species Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three North American PopSets (Peromyscus maniculatus, Sigmodon hispidus, and Urocitellus parryii; 3 × N = 36 = 108 conspecific isolates) benchmarked against *MAFFT, *IQ-TREE/*LSD2, *PAML codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4 The continental radiation of rodents (Order Rodentia) across North America via Paleogene Beringian corridors, Miocene grassland expansions, and Great American Biotic Interchange exchanges—coupled with the Anthropocene introduction of Old World commensal murids—established both the foundational small-mammal trophic guilds of Nearctic ecosystems and the primary sylvatic reservoirs for North America's major rodent-borne zoonoses. Here we execute a 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across an 18-locus, 64-species Glires supermatrix (L = 26,700 aligned columns with 7,979 parsimony-informative sites and 8,803 distinct site patterns) paired with independent 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) single-species Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three conspecific North American population datasets (3 × N = 36 = 108 isolates) benchmarking Native Rust against *MAFFT v7.526, *IQ-TREE v2.4.0 with *LSD2 v2.4.4, *PAML v4.10.10 codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4. Our fossil-calibrated chronogram anchors the Glires root (Lagomorpha vs. Rodentia) at 65.2 Ma, Crown Rodentia at 56.8 Ma, the Sciuromorpha–Castorimorpha split at 36.4 Ma, Myodonta (Dipodoidea vs. Muroidea) at 46.5 Ma, the Muridae–Cricetidae divergence at 24.8 Ma, Crown Cricetidae at 18.6 Ma, and the New World Neotominae–Sigmodontinae split at 13.4 Ma. Codon selection modeling (*PAML codeml) reveals strong purifying constraint on the Sin Nombre hantavirus endothelial receptor ITGB3 beta-3 integrin (omega = 0.5319), intermediate selective constraint on the high-altitude and fossorial hypoxia axis EPAS1/HBB (omega = 0.0343) and rodenticide-detoxification locus VKORC1/CYP2C (omega = 0.2572), and diversifying positive selection on bacterial pattern-recognition receptors TLR2/TLR4 (omega = 0.2631) and the New World Arenavirus receptor TFRC transferrin receptor 1 apical domain (omega = 0.1453). Across the three single-species PopSet skyline cohorts, we resolve post-glacial forest/oak-mast expansion and contemporary ENSO Sin Nombre hantavirus / Lyme disease amplification in the North American deer mouse (Peromyscus maniculatus, N = 36, Ne = 433,194 to 653,847; *BEAST = 667,970), northward agricultural grassland expansion and Black Creek Canal / Tamiami viral irruptions in the hispid cotton rat (Sigmodon hispidus, N = 36, Ne = 1,534,254 to 1,753,302; *BEAST = 1,808,005), and post-LGM Beringian steppe-tundra recolonization and high-latitude permafrost-thaw dynamics in the Arctic ground squirrel (Urocitellus parryii, N = 36, Ne = 707,606 to 1,687,680; *BEAST = 1,740,336), while demonstrating that Native Rust achieves a 42.9-fold end-to-end speedup (13.88 s vs. 595.24 s Hybrid and 1861.52 s full External UFBoot). research.abstract: Abstract Meiotic recombination ensures proper chromosome segregation and generates genetic variation among offspring. Recombination rates vary across taxa, with social Hymenoptera exhibiting some of the highest rates reported among multicellular animals, yet it remains an open question how such extreme recombination rates shape genome evolution. Here, we present a high-density linkage map for the California harvester ant Pogonomyrmex californicus and report an average genome-wide recombination rate of 14.73 cM/Mb, the highest documented for an ant to date. Recombination was strongly suppressed in gene-poor, repeat-rich regions and was positively associated with nucleotide diversity and genomic GC content. At the gene level, recombination rate was not associated with nonsynonymous substitution rate ( d N ) and showed no robust association with ω ( d N /d S ), providing little evidence that variation in local recombination rate is associated with detectable differences in selection efficacy among protein-coding genes. In contrast, synonymous substitution rate ( d S ) declined with recombination rate, whereas observed GC content at third codon positions (GC3) and inferred equilibrium GC content (GC3*) increased. These relationships persisted after accounting for gene-body methylation, which itself was negatively associated with recombination rate. Our results show that exceptionally high recombination rates are associated with variation in nucleotide diversity and base composition, with clear signatures of GC-biased sequence evolution.

research.abstract: AimsTo evaluate the effectiveness of GLP-1 RAs on clinical outcomes in diabetic patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). Methods and resultsIn this retrospective observational cohort study, all adults with diabetes mellitus and HFrEF between 2014 and 2025 were identified. Patients treated with GLP-1 RAs were matched to controls using stratified exact matching. The primary outcome was a composite of heart failure hospitalization or all-cause mortality. Treatment effects were estimated using nonparametric bootstrap resampling (1,000 iterations) to derive risk ratios, NNT estimates, and corresponding 95% confidence intervals. Time-to-event analyses using Cox proportional hazards models were performed as a validation analysis. Among 7,878 patients with HFrEF, 793 (10.1%) patients who initiated GLP-1 RA therapy after HF diagnosis were matched to 1,825 controls. GLP-1 receptor agonist use was associated with a lower risk of heart failure hospitalization or death, with risk ratios of 0.58 (95% CI: 0.42-0.77) at 12 months and 0.72 (95% CI: 0.61-0.85) at 36 months. The combination of high baseline event rates and substantial relative risk reduction translated into remarkably low NNT values in the overall population, with an NNT of 17 (95% CI: 11-33) at 1 year and 13 (95% CI: 8-25) at 3 years. Post hoc subgroup analyses demonstrated consistent effects across clinical subgroups, with no significant heterogeneity observed. ConclusionIn this large real-world cohort of diabetic patients with HFrEF, GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy, in addition to guideline-directed medical therapy, was associated with a lower risk of death or heart failure hospitalization. items.summary: UNLABELLED: The emergence of drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains presents a significant challenge to tuberculosis (TB) control programmes worldwide, particularly in high-burden countries, such as Pakistan. This study characterises the genomic diversity and drug resistance mutation profiles of M. tuberculosis isolates from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa using whole-genome sequencing (WGS). A…

research.abstract: UNLABELLED: The emergence of drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains presents a significant challenge to tuberculosis (TB) control programmes worldwide, particularly in high-burden countries, such as Pakistan. This study characterises the genomic diversity and drug resistance mutation profiles of M. tuberculosis isolates from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa using whole-genome sequencing (WGS). A total of 35 clinical M. tuberculosis isolates underwent WGS. Sequence data were quality-filtered and mapped to the H37Rv reference genome, characterising variants, including single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Lineage classification, drug resistance profiling, and identification of resistance mutations were performed using TB-Profiler software. SNP-based clustering was used to infer recent transmission events. All four major M. tuberculosis lineages (L1-L4) were detected; however, more than half of the isolates belonged to lineage L3 (CAS, n = 19; 54.3%). Almost all isolates were drug-resistant (34/35), including pre-extensively drug-resistant (pre-XDR, n = 15; 42.9%) and multidrug-resistant (MDR, n = 14; 40.0%) strains. The most frequent resistance-associated mutations included katG S315T (27/35) and inhA c.-777C > T (4/35) for isoniazid resistance, rpoB S450L (24/35) for rifampicin resistance, embB M306I/V (18/35) for ethambutol resistance, and gyrA D94G (8/35) and A90V (5/35) for fluoroquinolone resistance. Compensatory mutations were observed in rpoC and ahpC. Mutations associated with bedaquiline and clofazimine resistance (mmpR5 c.140dupA, c.138_139dupTG) were detected in single isolates. Interestingly, one isolate exhibited a deletion encompassing mmpR5, mmpL5, and mmpS5, potentially increasing bedaquiline susceptibility. Phylogenetic analysis using 6,635 genome-wide SNPs identified two transmission clusters with < 9 SNPs differences, suggesting ongoing local transmission. These results highlight the presence of drug-resistant M. tuberculosis strains in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, encompassing both globally recognised and novel resistance-associated mutations. Our findings underscore the critical need to integrate WGS into TB surveillance and control programmes in Pakistan to guide targeted interventions and curb the spread of resistant strains. research.abstract: ABSTRACT Animal species differ dramatically in their overall size, yet the mechanisms underlying these differences are poorly understood. The Hippo pathway, first discovered in Drosophila, and widely conserved in mammals, regulates the nuclear levels of YAP1, a transcriptional co-activator that enhances the expression of growth-promoting genes. While experimental manipulations of this pathway elicit dramatic effects on tissue growth and organ size, it is not known whether, and to what extent, evolutionary divergence of this pathway has contributed to size differences across animals. Here we show that although YAP1 protein sequence is highly conserved between diverse mammals such as humans, elephants and blue whales, it diverges considerably among rodent species. While the human YAP1 protein is very similar to that of the largest rodent, the capybara Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris, those of smaller rodents such as the mouse Mus musculus and the vole Microtus oregoni show considerable divergence. An increased ratio of non-synonymous versus synonymous substitutions (dN/dS) in clades of small rodents compared to the background is indicative of relaxed constraint in these lineages, suggesting relative positive selection. When expressed in the developing Drosophila wing, capybara YAP1 was more potent at promoting growth than that of the mouse or vole. Following transfection into mammalian cells, capybara YAP1 is more effective at promoting expression of a reporter gene than either mouse or vole YAP1. Thus, by combining computational and experimental approaches, we show that evolutionarily divergent coding-region changes in YAP1 have likely contributed to the evolution of smaller body size in clades of rodents.

items.title: Experimental evolution reveals temporally opposing roles for Csu pili during Acinetobacter baumannii respiratory infection
items.summary: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Acinetobacter baumannii is an opportunistic pathogen responsible for a wide range of infections, including ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream infections, and urinary tract infections. Most studies investigating A. baumannii pulmonary pathogenesis rely on acute pneumonia models that use high bacterial inocula and do not recapitulate the prolonged infections…

research.abstract: Abstract Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Acinetobacter baumannii is an opportunistic pathogen responsible for a wide range of infections, including ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream infections, and urinary tract infections. Most studies investigating A. baumannii pulmonary pathogenesis rely on acute pneumonia models that use high bacterial inocula and do not recapitulate the prolonged infections observed in some patients. Recently, our laboratory developed a murine model of chronic pulmonary infection that enabled the identification of virulence factors specifically required for long-term lung persistence. To investigate how A. baumannii adapts during chronic pulmonary infection, we performed an experimental evolution study using this model. This approach revealed an unexpected role for the archaic chaperone-usher (Csu) pili in A. baumannii pathogenesis. At early time points, Csu expression reduced bacterial burdens in both acute and chronic pneumonia models, an effect associated with enhanced host inflammatory responses. In contrast, at later stages of chronic infection, Csu promoted bacterial persistence, potentially by facilitating adhesion to pulmonary epithelial cells. These opposing effects were conserved across two distinct A. baumannii clinical isolates. We also found that Csu contributes to bacterial colonization in a catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) model in a strain-dependent manner. Together, these findings reveal an infection-stage-dependent role for Csu in A. baumannii pathogenesis, demonstrating that a bacterial surface structure can impair early colonization while promoting long-term persistence. Author summary Understanding how bacterial pathogens establish and maintain infections requires identifying the factors that promote their survival within the host. Currently, most experimental models of Acinetobacter baumannii infections focus on acute infections, potentially overlooking bacterial factors that are required for prolonged infections. In this study, we investigated how A. baumannii , a major cause of hospital-acquired infections, adapts to the lung environment during chronic infection. Using experimental evolution, we identified a novel role for Csu pili, surface structures traditionally associated with biofilm formation. Rather than promoting bacterial fitness throughout infection, Csu pili exhibited opposing effects depending on disease progression. Their expression was detrimental to bacterial fitness during early infection, a phenotype associated with increased host inflammatory responses, but became advantageous during prolonged infection, potentially by enhancing bacterial association with respiratory epithelial cells. Importantly, these opposing effects were observed in distinct clinical isolates, suggesting that this phenomenon is not restricted to a particular bacterial strain. Our findings highlight how the contribution of individual virulence factors can change over the course of infection and underscore the importance of considering infection duration when studying bacterial pathogenesis.

research.abstract: The metabolism of early microbes shaped our planet's chemistry and enabled more life to evolve. However, it remains uncertain when many forms of metabolism arose and which organisms carried them out. Here we combine machine learning, metabolic networks, and phylogenomics of microbes to date 14 forms of metabolism and 6 other traits. We find that metabolism evolved in three waves, starting >3.4 billion years ago (Ga) with fermentation and sulfur compound respiration. A second wave began ~3.2 Ga with aerobic respiration and growth, while a third began ~1.4 Ga with further specialization. We compared these predictions with independent dates from the geochemical record, and agreement with conservative dates was good (CCC = 0.81 to 0.89). Several forms of metabolism are invisible in the geochemical record, and our approach dates these forms, too. Our results reconcile different lines of evidence for microbial evolution and provide a fuller picture of early Earth.

Such strategies will likely involve the use of liquid biopsies, which can analyze biomarkers found in blood for the presence of cancer. We introduce Blackjack, a new detection…

research.abstract: Abstract Current cancer screening efforts face the dual problems of low patient adherence and a lack of available tests for many cancers, which motivates the development of less invasive multi-cancer early detection strategies. Such strategies will likely involve the use of liquid biopsies, which can analyze biomarkers found in blood for the presence of cancer. We introduce Blackjack, a new detection approach that focuses on the fragmentation patterns of plasma-derived cell-free DNA (cfDNA). Blackjack characterizes a person’s cfDNA fragmentation sites with a position probability matrix (PPM) that encodes information about the sequence context of the sites. For classification, Blackjack computes two features that represent the similarity of an individual’s PPM to those of known healthy and cancer cohorts. With these two features, Blackjack then uses logistic regression to classify a new sample as being from a healthy individual or a person with cancer. In cross-validation experiments using two external whole genome sequencing datasets, Blackjack showed high performance, achieving a minimum area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.993 and minimum sensitivity (Sn) of 91.8% (at 98% specificity). This high performance was also present for stage I (AUC 0.991, Sn 89.8%) and stage II cancers (AUC 0.993, Sn 90.2%), and across eight different cancers (minimum AUC 0.985, minimum Sn 80.0%). We demonstrate that Blackjack’s accuracy is stable at low simulated sequencing depths (∼0.24x), and that tissue of origin prediction using Blackjack’s similarity measures is high (minimum 82% accuracy of the top two predicted tissues). Our findings show that cfDNA fragmentation site contexts have valuable signals for early cancer detection, and that developing diagnostics with machine learning can benefit from a focus on having a small number of informative features.

Here, we demonstrate that R-pyocins (phage-like bactericidal particles) can be leveraged…

research.abstract: Abstract The global escalation of antibiotic resistance is a critical threat necessitating innovative strategies to provide new therapeutic options and restore the efficacy of conventional drugs. Pseudomonas aeruginosa exemplifies this challenge by utilizing a robust genomic resistome to persist in clinical settings. Here, we demonstrate that R-pyocins (phage-like bactericidal particles) can be leveraged not as conventional biocides but as precise selective forces to drive an evolutionary trap. We subjected the laboratory strains PAO1 and PAK and the clinical pan-drug-resistant (PDR) wound isolate MRSN 6220 to R-pyocin selective pressure. Under sustained R-pyocin pressure, every pyomelanogenic variant we recovered evaded R-pyocin killing through large-scale chromosomal deletions spanning 250-388 kbp. These deletions encompass a conserved region harboring the galU gene (essential for LPS synthesis), the hmgA gene (yielding a pyomelanogenic ‘brown’ phenotype), and the mexXYZ multidrug efflux operon. While the loss of galU confers broad cross-resistance to R-pyocins by likely truncating the LPS receptor, the concurrent excision of mexXY induces profound collateral sensitivity to aminoglycosides. These deletions also eliminate critical virulence factors and biofilm clusters, including the hcnABC , exoY , phzABCDEFG , and cup operons. In a Galleria mellonella model, the resulting brown mutants were non-lethal, and in infected murine wound tissue treated ex vivo with gentamicin they exhibited a significant 3-log reduction in bacterial load, whereas the pan-drug-resistant ancestor did not. This work establishes a framework for utilizing R-pyocins as evolutionary steering agents that couple the acquisition of R-pyocin resistance to the reversion of multidrug resistance into an attenuated, biofilm-deficient, and clinically manageable state. Importance Pan-drug-resistant (PDR) pathogens demand novel strategies that both kill and restore antibiotic efficacy. Here, we describe an evolutionary trap for Pseudomonas aeruginosa , where selection for R-pyocin resistance drives large-scale (∼300 kb) chromosomal remodeling. Although these deletions confer R-pyocin immunity via loss of the galU gene, they simultaneously collapse the pathogen’s virulence and defense. Crucially, the excision of the mexXY efflux operon resensitizes a PDR clinical isolate to conventional aminoglycosides, while the collateral loss of critical virulence and biofilm clusters abrogates pathogenesis. By coupling resistance acquisition to substantial fitness costs, our work establishes a framework for using R-pyocins to force predictable evolutionary trade-offs, driving the reversion of multidrug resistance to an attenuated, biofilm-deficient, and clinically manageable state.

items.title: Decoding positive selection in Mycobacterium tuberculosis with phylogeny-guided graph attention models.
items.summary: MOTIVATION: Positive selection is a key evolutionary force in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, driving the emergence of adaptive mutations that influence drug resistance, transmissibility, and virulence of tuberculosis. Phylogenetic trees capture the hierarchical evolutionary relationships among isolates, making them an ideal framework for detecting such adaptive signals. Here, we present a…

research.abstract: Abstract Motivation Positive selection is a key evolutionary force in Mycobacterium tuberculosis , driving the emergence of adaptive mutations that influence drug resistance, transmissibility, and virulence of tuberculosis. Phylogenetic trees capture the hierarchical evolutionary relationships among isolates, making them an ideal framework for detecting such adaptive signals. Here, we present a phylogeny-guided graph attention network approach, coupled with a novel method for converting SNP-annotated phylogenetic trees into graph structures suitable for graph neural network processing. Results Using a dataset of 1000 M. tuberculosis isolates, representing the four main lineages, and 206 single-nucleotide variants (75 resistance-associated and 131 neutral) spanning 79 drug-resistance genes, we constructed graphs where nodes represented individual isolates and edges reflected phylogenetic distances. To reduce noise and highlight local evolutionary structure, we pruned edges between isolates separated by more than seven internal nodes. Node features were encoded as binary indicators of SNP presence or absence, and the graph attention network (GAT) architecture comprised two attention layers with a residual connection, followed by global attention pooling and a multilayer perceptron classifier. The model achieved higher accuracy (0.81, AUC 0.82) than a homoplasy-count baseline (0.71) on the held-out test set. Under repeated cross-validation, however, F1 scores did not differ significantly (0.56 vs. 0.58; paired Wilcoxon p = 0.98), reflecting a specificity-sensitivity trade-off: the GAT favoured specificity (0.89), the baseline favoured sensitivity. Applying the model to 138 WHO-classified “uncertain” variants identified 28 high-confidence candidates, including rpoC Ile491Val (rifampicin, compensatory), ubiA Arg240Cys (ethambutol), and rpsA Ala412Val (pyrazinamide). These findings demonstrate the feasibility of encoding phylogenetic trees as graph neural network-compatible structures and the utility of attention-based models for detecting positive-selection signals, supporting genomic surveillance and prioritisation of candidates for experimental validation. Availability and Implementation The source code for the model can be found at https://github.com/linfeng-wang/Phylogeny-Guided_GAT .

research.abstract: 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across 64 species and 16 loci (L = 23,924 aligned columns; African Catarrhini and Neotropical Pitheciidae, Atelidae, Cebidae, Callitrichidae, and Aotidae) coupled with 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three independent PopSets (Alouatta spp., Sapajus/Cebus, and Callithrix/Saguinus/Leontopithecus) benchmarked against *MAFFT, *IQ-TREE/*LSD2, *PAML codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4 The colonization of South America by African anthropoid primates during the Middle to Late Eocene and their subsequent diversification across Neotropical forest strata into five ecologically specialized families (Pitheciidae, Atelidae, Cebidae, Callitrichidae, and Aotidae) represent one of mammalogy's classic trans-oceanic adaptive radiations. Here we execute a 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across a 16-locus, 64-species primate supermatrix (L = 23,924 aligned columns with 10,254 parsimony-informative sites and 11,093 distinct site patterns) coupled with independent 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three localized Neotropical population datasets benchmarking Native Rust against *MAFFT v7.526, *IQ-TREE v2.4.0 with *LSD2 v2.4.4, *PAML v4.10.10 codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4. Our fossil-calibrated chronogram anchors Crown Primates at 74.0 Ma, the trans-Atlantic Simiiformes split between African Catarrhini (crown 28.5 Ma) and Neotropical Platyrrhini at 43.2 Ma (stem rafting window 43.2–24.2 Ma across the Eocene Atlantic), and Crown Platyrrhini at 24.2 Ma, followed by crown radiations of Pitheciidae (19.8 Ma), Atelidae (16.8 Ma), Cebidae (19.5 Ma), Callitrichidae (14.8 Ma), and Aotidae (11.4 Ma). Codon selection modeling (*PAML codeml) reveals strong purifying constraint on Pro8-oxytocin OXT/OXTR neuroendocrine signaling (omega = 0.4905), intermediate selective constraint on TAS2R bitter-taste receptors (omega = 0.7442) and ENAM/GHR dental and phyletic-dwarfism loci (omega = 0.8436), and diversifying and balancing selection on duplicated RNASE1/CHIA folivory-insectivory digestive enzymes (omega = 1.2118) and X-linked OPN1LW spectral-tuning opsin exons (omega = 2.4891). Across the three localized PopSet skyline cohorts, we resolve late Quaternary trans-Andean expansion and contemporary yellow fever epizootic pressure in howler monkeys (Alouatta, Ne = 628,056 to 977,186; *BEAST = 1,007,674), Pleistocene Cerrado/Caatinga dry-corridor colonization and stone-tool nut-cracking persistence in capuchins (Sapajus/Cebus, Ne = 1,042,598 to 1,376,278; *BEAST = 1,411,397), and Atlantic Forest fragmentation followed by metapopulation translocation recovery in callitrichid marmosets and tamarins (Callithrix/Saguinus/Leontopithecus, Ne = 469,859 to 912,085; *BEAST = 940,542), while demonstrating that Native Rust achieves a 29.9-fold end-to-end speedup (13.54 s vs. 404.82 s Hybrid and 3127.88 s full External UFBoot). research.abstract: Abstract Background The HSP70 family maintains cellular proteostasis and mediates vertebrate responses to environmental stress. The Chinese alligator ( Alligator sinensis ), an ectothermic crocodilian, undergoes winter dormancy characterized by cessation of feeding, reduced activity, and metabolic depression. However, the evolutionary patterns of the HSP70 family across vertebrates and their potential relevance to winter dormancy in crocodilians remain poorly understood. We characterized the HSP70 family across 24 vertebrate species, focusing on the molecular evolution of HSPA12A along crocodilian lineages and its seasonal expression in the hypothalamus of the Chinese alligator. Results Using HMMER- and BLAST-based searches, we identified 355 HSP70 family members, with 11–28 members per species. Phylogenetic, synteny, and subcellular localization analyses indicated that the family is broadly conserved but exhibits subfamily- and lineage-associated divergence. Under two foreground schemes in which the terminal branches of two winter-dormant crocodilians or all four crocodilian species were jointly designated as foreground, HSPA12A showed an elevated relative evolutionary rate and significant evidence of positive selection. HyPhy aBSREL supported episodic diversifying selection on the A. sinensis HSPA12A terminal branch. Public RNA-seq data showed that HSPA12A expression was highest in the hypothalamus among sampled female tissues and was higher in winter than in summer (600.0 and 329.2 TPM, respectively). Western blotting and immunofluorescence analyses showed descriptive differences between the examined specimens, with higher HSPA12A protein abundance and a higher density of cells double-positive for anti-HSPA12A antibody immunoreactivity and NeuN in winter. Because each RNA-seq, western blotting, and immunofluorescence comparison included only one biological specimen per season, these observations were treated as descriptive, and no inferential statistical comparisons were performed. Conclusions The vertebrate HSP70 family is broadly conserved but shows differentiation among subfamilies and lineages. The evolutionary analyses indicate a broader crocodilian-lineage-associated pattern of HSPA12A evolution that cannot be attributed specifically to winter dormancy. Separately, the descriptive transcriptomic and preliminary protein-level observations provide a basis for considering HSPA12A as a candidate for further investigation in relation to winter physiology in the Chinese alligator. These findings do not establish winter dormancy as the selective driver of HSPA12A evolution, and its biological function and causal role remain to be determined.

research.abstract: Camelids have evolved remarkable physiological adaptations enabling survival in extreme desert environments, yet the genomic basis of these traits remains incompletely understood. We conducted a comparative genomic analysis across eleven mammalian species, including three Old World camels, four New World camels, two additional artiodactyls (pig, cattle), and two outgroups (human, mouse), to identify lineage-specific molecular signatures of adaptation. Using OrthoFinder, we constructed orthologous gene families and identified 11,861 single-copy orthologs across all species. We detected significant copy-number changes in cytochrome P450 gene families, with expansion of CYP2J and contraction of CYP4F in the camelid ancestor, suggesting a shift toward anti-inflammatory eicosanoid signaling. Branch-site analyses identified 47 high-confidence positively selected genes in Old World camels, including HACD3, a fatty acid elongation enzyme harboring an ultraconserved substitution (D270N). Structural modeling and conservation analysis suggest that this substitution may hypothetically alter protein conformation, but this prediction awaits experimental validation. Tissue-specific RNA-seq analysis confirmed that HACD3 is expressed in camel kidney and liver, tissues central to lipid metabolism and water conservation. Systematic screening for inactivating mutations identified ten high-confidence pseudogenized genes, including CES3, CPA3, and PLA2G2F, enriched in lipid metabolism and epidermal pathways. The adaptive significance of these losses is currently hypothetical and inferred from homologous gene studies in mice and humans; because some of the cited genes are paralogs rather than orthologs, and because mouse and human phenotypes may not transfer to camels, these inferences are hypothesis-generating only and do not establish camel gene function. Experimental validation confirmed pseudogenization of TAS2R16, and cell-based calcium-signalling assays showed that the camel receptor fails to respond to salicin. This establishes loss of receptor function but not its adaptive significance; both dietary-breadth and neutral (relaxed-selection or drift) explanations remain compatible with the data. For CES3, CPA3, and PLA2G2F, functional consequences in camels remain unverified and require camel-specific experimental validation. Collectively, these results provide a comprehensive framework of gene family evolution, positive selection, and gene loss underlying desert adaptation in camelids, while highlighting that expression patterns are correlative only and do not demonstrate that the identified variants alter protein function or physiology.

research.abstract: Abstract Thienothiazolocarboxamides (TTCs) were discovered as a hit in a whole cell screen for new antituberculosis agents. These molecules were rapidly cidal under both replicating and non-replicating conditions and killed Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) in macrophages. The heterobicyclic core of this scaffold was essential for activity and resistance to these agents was mediated by loss of EthA, a flavin containing monooxygenase also responsible for the bioactivation of ethionamide. EthA-mediated activation of TTCs in whole cells was found to produce mycothiol adducts and RNAseq profiles revealed a mechanism of action identical to the fungal mycotoxins patulin and nidulalin A. EthA oxidizes the sulfur of the thiazole ring to create a relatively stable sulfenic acid that reacts with cellular thiols. This unique, replication-independent, mechanism suggests the possibility that these molecules may contribute significantly to shortening the duration of tuberculosis chemotherapy.

research.abstract: Abstract CRISPR-based lineage recording technologies can trace the ancestry of hundreds of thousands of cells, yet reconstructing accurate phylogenies at this scale remains computationally challenging. Likelihood-based methods employ explicit evolutionary models of CRISPR editing that improve tree accuracy but require computationally expensive searches over tree topologies, whereas greedy distance-based alternatives scale efficiently but their accuracy requires distances that faithfully represent the true phylogeny. Here, we introduce HERACLES, which optimizes cell coordinates in hyperbolic space under a quartet-based composite likelihood of CRISPR editing. By recovering local branching structures directly from embedded distances, HERACLES guides continuous optimization with an explicit evolutionary model without repeatedly constructing and evaluating complete phylogenies. Across simulated benchmarks, HERACLES improves reconstruction accuracy over existing methods and scales to lineages containing 150,000 cells in about four hours on a single GPU. On experimental KP-tracer and PEtracer datasets, HERACLES reconstructs phylogenies consistent with independent anatomical annotations and temporal lineage markers. Its flexible likelihood framework also accommodates different recording mechanisms, and incorporating sequential editing improves reconstruction of simulated DNA Typewriter lineages. Together, these results establish continuous optimization of local evolutionary relationships as a scalable and flexible approach to probabilistic lineage reconstruction. Code availability HERACLES is available at https://github.com/morrislab/HERACLES .

research.abstract: Background: Rare coding variants contribute to cardiovascular disease, but their effects across disease groups remain incompletely characterized. In particular, the influence of functionally and clinically informed variant classification and sex-specific genetic effects on gene-phenotype associations remains understudied. Methods: We analyzed whole-genome sequencing data from up to 483,311 UK Biobank participants across six genetic ancestry groups and eight cardiovascular phenotype groups. Gene-burden testing integrated state-of-the-art missense classification and predicted pathogenic germline variants. We performed combined-sex and sex-stratified analyses, followed by cross-ancestry meta-analysis. We additionally adjusted for cardiometabolic traits in sensitivity analyses, estimated penetrance among qualifying-variant carriers, and assessed genetic prevalence across eight ancestry groups. Results: We identified 86 exome-wide significant gene-phenotype associations: 40 established and 46 novel. Novel associations included EHMT2 with atrial fibrillation, P2RX1 with arrhythmias, P2RY4 with complete atrioventricular block, and NOSTRIN with atherosclerotic heart disease in females. After cardiometabolic adjustment, 60 associations retained exome-wide significance and 18 additional associations emerged, including CDH11, PARVA, and ADAMDEC1 with atherosclerosis-related phenotypes. Conclusions: These findings identify novel cardiovascular gene-phenotype associations implicating purinergic signaling, endothelial nitric oxide regulation, and vascular wall biology. Variant selection shapes penetrance estimates and the interpretation of inherited susceptibility.

research.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based computer-aided detection (CAD) of tuberculosis (TB) on chest X-ray (CXR) may standardize screening and triage in settings with few radiologists but its accuracy in clinical cohorts remains uncertain. We searched five databases (PubMed, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, OpenAlex, Lens.org) on 15 March 2026 for studies published between January 2020 and March 2026, and we appraised these studies using QUADAS-2. Evaluations from clinical cohorts with complete 2 x 2 data and a microbiological or composite reference standard for all participants were pooled using a bivariate random-effects model, with 95% prediction intervals. We accounted for overlapping participants by performing a post hoc analysis with one evaluation per cohort and used GRADE to assess the certainty of the evidence. No protocol was prepared or registered. We included 21 studies (26 evaluations of AI models). Nine evaluations from three independent cohorts were pooled. Pooled sensitivity was 0.896 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.874 to 0.915, prediction interval 0.798 to 0.950) and pooled specificity was 0.689 (95% CI 0.642 to 0.732; prediction interval 0.499 to 0.831). Both confidence intervals include the World Health Organization (WHO) triage thresholds (sensitivity 90%, specificity 70%). When a screening study with partial verification was added, pooled specificity increased to 0.735. Eighteen of 24 assessed evaluations were at high risk of bias and only 1 of 21 studies was prospective, fully verified, externally validated and met the WHO thresholds. Certainty of evidence was low for sensitivity and very low for specificity. A subsequent PubMed search found additional eligible clinical evaluations that were not screened, so the review is incomplete for those studies. In clinical cohorts, AI-CXR sensitivity is close to the WHO triage target, and specificity is close to, but not clearly above, its target. The evidence is pooled across only three cohorts, and specificity varies by product and setting. Thresholds need to be calibrated locally, and prospective, externally validated evaluations are needed before widespread deployment.

research.abstract: **Abstract** **Background** Young adults with type 1 diabetes (T1D) in low- and middle-income countries experience persistently poor glycaemic control despite improved insulin access. Evidence on the effects of social determinants of health (SDOH) on glycaemic control, complications, and psychological well-being remains limited, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. We examined relationships between SDOH, psychological health, glycaemic control, and early complication markers among young adults with T1D in Kenya. **Methods** We conducted a multicentre cross-sectional study among 164 adults aged 18-34 years attending four diabetes clinics in Kenya. SDOH were assessed using a prespecified, context-informed questionnaire covering six domains. Psychological well-being was assessed using PAID, PHQ-9, and GAD-7. Clinical outcomes included HbA1c, a single urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR), and lipid profile. Associations between SDOH domains and clinical and psychological outcomes were evaluated using multivariable ordinal and binary logistic regression models adjusted for age, sex, and diabetes duration. **Findings** Mean age was 24.96+/-4.35 years and diabetes duration 7.26+/-5.70 years. Mean HbA1c was 11.5+/-3.44%, with only 4.9% achieving <7%. LDL cholesterol was above target in 56.1%, 64.0% had an elevated LDL/HDL ratio, and 28.0% had elevated UACR. Diabetes distress and clinically significant depressive symptoms affected 30.5% and 27.5%, respectively. Moderate-to-high SDOH burden was greatest for economic stability (76.8%), social/community context (52.4%), and food environment (43.9%). All SDOH domains showed positive but non-significant associations with HbA1c. Diabetes distress was associated with economic instability (aOR 1.42, 95% CI 1.17-1.72), healthcare system burden (1.45, 1.12-1.87), neighbourhood/physical environment burden (1.39, 1.07-1.80), and food environment burden (1.30, 1.03-1.64). Anxiety was associated with social/community (1.70, 1.14-2.53) and healthcare system burden (1.68, 1.19-2.36). Economic instability was associated with elevated UACR (1.40, 1.05-1.85). **Discussion** Young adults with T1D in Kenya experience substantial social and psychological burden alongside poor glycaemic control and early complication markers. Social disadvantage appears to influence kidney disease complications, and psychological well-being regardless of glycaemic control in our sample, underscoring the need to move beyond glucose-centered care. Poor glycaemic control was pervasive, which likely obviated any detectable differences by SDOH in this population. Ultimately, Integrated care addressing SDOH and mental health may support more sustainable long-term outcomes. Key words: Type 1 diabetes; Social determinants; glycemic control; complications, psychological health

research.abstract: Abstract Mussels belonging to the genus Mytilus are among the world’s most ecologically and economically important bivalve molluscs. Although the genus most likely originated in the Northern Hemisphere, the evolutionary history of Southern Hemisphere lineages, including the timing and number of colonisation events leading to the extant Australian populations, remains debated. Limited genomic resources have hindered the reconstruction of these evolutionary histories. In Australia, distinguishing native Mytilus planulatus from invasive Mytilus galloprovincialis is critical for biosecurity and conservation, but previous molecular approaches lacked sufficient resolution to resolve species boundaries and hybridisation patterns. Here, we present the first chromosome-scale reference genome for M. planulatus . The assembly consists of 14 chromosomes and over 51,000 annotated protein-coding genes per haplotype. Comparative analysis revealed extensive structural variation and widespread hemizygosity despite a largely conserved chromosomal organisation relative to M. galloprovincialis . Population analyses using SNPs and gene presence-absence variation in resequenced individuals confirmed previously inferred patterns of population structure and establish this reference genome as a valuable resource for future studies of genome evolution, adaptation and population genomics in Mytilus .

research.abstract: Abstract Purpose We introduce GraNPA (Graph Node-Phenotype Association), a method that performs a phenotype-sequence association analysis on a pangenome variation graph (PVG). This PVG is built using a small number of individual genome sequences and does not require additional population materials or kinship information for qualitative phenotypes. This approach minimizes the number of individuals required for association studies and mitigates the impact of reference bias in variant calling within these types of analyses. Background A PVG is a representation of the multiple alignment of a set of complete genomes. It contains all variations, ranging from single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) to large structural variations (SVs), and these are represented as nodes in the graph. By integrating phenotype information within these nodes, we can assign a Score ( S ) to each one and identify regions related to the phenotype directly within the PVG. These regions represent statistically significant shifts in S distribution, indicating their involvement in the phenotype. Finally, GraNPA provides their positions and scores for further analysis. Results This method was tested using different simulated contexts and two publicly available datasets: the Sub1A gene locus for Asian rice Oryza sativa in a 13 individuals PVG, and the insertion responsible for the white-headed in cattle ( Bos taurus ) with a PVG of 24 individuals. Source code of GraNPA is available here https://forge.ird.fr/diade/graphgwas/granpa under GNU GPLv3. Conclusion GraNPA was able to identify the expected area in two simulated datasets, as well as the loci responsible for these two known traits, using only a few dozen complete genomes from these PVGs. Although this method is currently limited to qualitative phenotypes, it paves the way for more efficient methods that rely on PVGs and a small number of individuals.

research.abstract: Abstract Fragmentomics analyzes features of circulating cell-free DNA fragments (e.g., fragment length or end motifs) derived from whole-genome sequencing of liquid biopsy samples (blood or other body fluids), enabling non-invasive early cancer detection. Here we present mFrag, a framework that integrates external methylation reference atlases with fragmentomic features for lung cancer detection. mFrag comprises two complementary methods: mFrag-Weight, which uses DNA methylation information to weight fragmentomic features, and mFrag-Net, which integrates fragmentomic features and external DNA methylation data through neural networks. We average the output probabilities of the two methods to obtain a final prediction score. The mFrag model was trained using 287 individuals at risk for lung cancer. In an independent case-control testing set comprising 385 non-cancer controls and 46 cancers (28 stage I, 12 stage II, and 6 stage III or IV), mFrag outperforms a DELFI-style fragmentomic approach, improving PR-AUC from 0.455 to 0.720 and sensitivity at 99% specificity from 0.043 to 0.478, with ROC-AUC from 0.871 to 0.908. For stage I lung cancer, mFrag raises PR-AUC from 0.314 to 0.558 and ROC-AUC from 0.855 to 0.894. Applied to end 4-mer motif features, mFrag likewise improved over an unweighted baseline, with gains contributed by both mFrag-Weight and mFrag-Net. In summary, mFrag improves the accuracy of fragmentomics-based lung cancer detection through integrating external DNA methylation data and the complementarity of its two component models, without incurring any additional data-generating cost.

research.abstract: Abstract Colored k -mer indexes record, for every k -mer of a collection of genomes, the genomes or species that contain it, and underpin pseudoalignment and sequence search against large collections. Construction of such an index is expensive, yet the collection it represents is rarely final: genomes are retracted or found to be contaminated, users need an index of a single species or clade, and new genomes keep arriving. Rebuilding the index after every such change requires the original sequences and repeats the costly construction. We show that colored indexes based on the spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform (SBWT) can instead be updated efficiently in batches, without the original sequences, and with a result equivalent to the index built from scratch. Given an SBWT and any subset of its k -mers, we first extract the SBWT of this subset directly from the input, in one linear pass and without building a new index. Removing genomes, intersection and difference all reduce to this operation. We then carry the colors through every operation, by finding from the inputs alone where the color sets of the result change, so that removing or extracting genomes, as well as the union, intersection and difference of two colored indexes, each directly yield a complete colored index. In our experiments, editing paid off for large results: removing a genome from an index of 3 682 E. coli genomes took 54 seconds instead of 13 minutes for a rebuild, and adding one took about a minute. On AllTheBacteria, with 192 billion k -mers and 12 733 species, extracting M. tuberculosis , with 180 094 genomes, took less than four hours, and set operations then traced contamination of its color, some of which the next release of AllTheBacteria still contains. Our work turns large colored k -mer indexes from static snapshots of a collection into resources that can be maintained as the collection evolves. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/LoreDepuydt/colored-sbwt-setops .
